e: Chapter V deals with the Child Welfare Committee.

q: Which Chapter of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 deals with the procedure in relation to children in need of care and protection?
e: Chapter VI covers the procedure in relation to children in need of care and protection.

q: Which Chapter of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 deals with Rehabilitation and Social Reintegration?
e: Chapter VII covers Rehabilitation and Social Reintegration.

q: Which Chapter of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 deals with Adoption?
e: Chapter VIII of the Act deals with Adoption.

q: Which Chapter of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 deals with Other Offences Against Children?
e: Chapter IX covers Other Offences Against Children.

q: Which Chapter of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 is the 'Miscellaneous' chapter?
e: Chapter X is the Miscellaneous chapter, the last of the Act's 10 chapters.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, a 'child' is defined under which section as anyone below 18 years of age?
e: Section 2(35) defines a child as anyone below 18 years of age.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, 'child in conflict with law' is defined under which section?
e: Section 2(13) defines a 'child in conflict with law'.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, 'child in need of care and protection' is defined under which section?
e: Section 2(14) defines 'child in need of care and protection'.

q: As per the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, a 'child in conflict with law' is a child below 18 years who:
o: Is alleged to have committed an offense
Is a victim of sexual abuse
e: A 'child in conflict with law' is a child below 18 years of age who is alleged to have committed an offense.

q: Which two bodies operate in every district under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 to work for children requiring care and protection?
o: Juvenile Justice Board and Child Welfare Committee
District Magistrate and State Adoption Resource Agency
Special Juvenile Police Unit and Childline
Child Protection Society and Probation Office
e: The Juvenile Justice Board (JJB) and the Child Welfare Committee (CWC) operate in all districts for children needing care and protection.

q: As per the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, 'After Care' [Section 2(5)] applies to young people who have completed 18 years but have not yet turned:
e: After Care helps young people achieve self-sufficiency between 18 and 21 years of age, including financial assistance.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, who serves as the chairperson of the District Child Protection Unit?
o: The Chairperson of the Child Welfare Committee
e: The District Child Protection Unit, constituted under Section 106, has the District Magistrate as its chairperson.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, 'Fit Person' is defined under which section?
e: Section 2(28) defines 'Fit Person' as any individual prepared to take responsibility for a child for a specific purpose.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, 'Fit Facility' is defined under which section?
e: Section 2(27) defines a 'Fit Facility' as a facility run by a government institution, registered voluntary organization, or NGO willing to temporarily take responsibility for a child.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, 'Probation Officer' is defined under which section?
e: Section 2(48) defines a Probation Officer as an officer appointed under the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958, or a legal-probation officer appointed under the District Child Protection Unit.

q: Under which Act is a Probation Officer (as referenced in the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015) appointed by the State Government?
o: The Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956
e: A Probation Officer is appointed by the State Government under the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, 'Special Juvenile Police Unit' is defined under which section?
e: Section 2(55) defines the Special Juvenile Police Unit.

q: As per the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, allowing a child who cannot stay with their biological family or be given for adoption to be temporarily placed with another family is called:
e: This arrangement is called Foster Care.

q: Which section of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 lays down the general principles to be followed in implementing the Act?
e: Section 3 lays down the general principles to be followed while implementing the provisions of the Act.

q: As per the general principles under Section 3 of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, placing a child in institutional care should be:
o: Considered only as a last resort
Mandatory for all children in conflict with law
e: Institutional care should be considered only as a last resort, after a fair inquiry.

q: As per the general principles under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, can a child waive their rights under the Act, even at their own request?
o: Yes, if approved by the Board
No, a waiver of the child's rights is not permissible
e: A waiver of the child's rights is not permissible even if requested by the child or someone acting on their behalf.

q: Which section of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 deals with the constitution of the Juvenile Justice Board?
e: Section 4 deals with the constitution of the Juvenile Justice Board in every district.

q: As per the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, what is the minimum experience required for the Principal Magistrate on the Juvenile Justice Board?
e: The Principal Magistrate (Metropolitan/First Class Judicial/Chief Judicial Magistrate) must have at least 3 years of experience.

q: How many Social Workers are included as members of the Juvenile Justice Board under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015?
o: Two, at least one a woman
e: The Board includes two Social Workers, at least one of whom must be a woman.

q: As per the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, a social worker can be appointed to the Juvenile Justice Board only if they have been actively involved in child health, education, or welfare activities for at least:
e: A social worker must have at least 7 years of active involvement in child-related health, education, or welfare activities, or hold a relevant professional degree.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, which of the following is a disqualification for Juvenile Justice Board membership?
o: Having a past history of violating human or child rights
e: A person with a past history of violating human rights or child rights is disqualified from board membership.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, within how many days of appointment must induction training and sensitization be provided to all Juvenile Justice Board members?
e: Induction training must be provided to all Board members, including the Principal Magistrate, within 60 days of appointment.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, a Juvenile Justice Board member (other than the Principal Magistrate) can be terminated for failing to attend Board proceedings for how many consecutive months without valid reason?
e: A member can be terminated for failing to attend proceedings for three consecutive months without valid reason.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, a Board member can also be terminated for failing to attend at least what fraction of sittings in a year?
e: A member can be terminated for failing to attend at least three-fourths of the sittings in a year.

q: As per Section 5 of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, if a child under inquiry turns 18 during the inquiry process, that person shall be treated as:
o: An adult, and the inquiry transferred to a regular court
A child, and the inquiry continued
Referred to the Children's Court automatically
e: Under Section 5, the person continues to be treated as a child and the inquiry is continued, notwithstanding turning 18.

q: As per Section 6 of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, a person apprehended after turning 18 for an offence committed when they were under 18 shall be treated, during the inquiry, as:
e: Section 6 provides that such a person shall be treated as a child during the inquiry process.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, how many members, at minimum, must be present at the final disposal of a case by the Juvenile Justice Board, and who must be among them?
o: Two members, including the Principal Magistrate
Three members, including the Principal Magistrate
e: At final disposal, at least two members, including a Principal Magistrate, must be present.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, if there is no majority opinion among Board members on a matter, whose opinion prevails?
o: The matter is referred to the Children's Court
e: If there is no majority, the opinion of the Principal Magistrate prevails.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, within how many days of a child first being produced before the Board must the social investigation report be submitted?
e: A social investigation report must be submitted within 15 days from the date the child is first produced before the Board.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, who conducts the social investigation to find the circumstances of an alleged offence, in the absence of a Probation Officer?
o: A Child Welfare Officer or a social worker
e: In the absence of a Probation Officer, a Child Welfare Officer or a social worker undertakes the social investigation.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, what must a Magistrate not empowered under the Act do upon forming an opinion that an accused person is a child?
o: Record the opinion and forward the child with case records to the Board having jurisdiction
Refer the matter to the Supreme Court
e: The Magistrate must record the opinion and forward the child, with records of proceedings, to the Board having jurisdiction.

q: Which section of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 deals with the apprehension of a child alleged to be in conflict with law?
e: Section 10 deals with apprehension of a child alleged to be in conflict with law.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, within how many hours of apprehension must a child alleged to be in conflict with law be produced before the Juvenile Justice Board?
e: The child must be produced before the Board within 24 hours of apprehension.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, can a child alleged to be in conflict with law be placed in a police lock-up or jail?
o: Yes, if no observation home is available
e: Under no circumstances shall such a child be placed in a police lock-up or jail.

q: Which section of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 deals with the inquiry by the Board regarding a child in conflict with law?
e: Section 14 deals with the Board's inquiry regarding a child in conflict with law.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, within how many months must the Board's inquiry regarding a child in conflict with law be completed?
e: The inquiry must be completed within 4 months from the date the child is produced before the Board.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, within how many months must the Board complete a preliminary assessment for heinous crimes?
e: Preliminary assessments for heinous crimes must be completed within 3 months from the date the child is first produced.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, who may grant an extension of time for the Board's inquiry into a serious or heinous crime?
o: The Chief Judicial Magistrate or Chief Metropolitan Magistrate
e: An extension may be granted by the Chief Judicial Magistrate or Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, for reasons recorded in writing.

q: Under Section 15 of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, a preliminary assessment of mental and physical capacity is required if a child of what age or above commits a heinous crime?
e: If a child who has completed 16 years of age or above commits a heinous crime, the Board conducts a preliminary assessment under Section 15.

q: Which section of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 deals with the powers of the Children's Court?
e: Section 19 deals with the powers of the Children's Court.

q: As per Section 21 of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, what sentence can NOT be given to a child in conflict with law under this Act or any other law?
e: Section 21 prohibits the death sentence or life imprisonment for any child in conflict with law.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, until what age must a child in conflict with law sent to a place of safety be kept there before transfer to jail?
e: The Children's Court must ensure the child is sent to a place of safety until they reach 21 years, after which they are transferred to jail.

q: Which section of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 deals with the Child Welfare Committee?
e: Section 27 deals with the constitution of the Child Welfare Committee.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, within how many months of notification must induction training be given to Child Welfare Committee members?
e: Induction training and awareness must be provided to CWC members within two months from the date of notification.

q: As per the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, what is the total composition of a Child Welfare Committee?
o: A Chairperson and two other members
A Chairperson and three other members
A Chairperson and four other members
A Chairperson and five other members
e: The CWC consists of a Chairperson and four other members, with at least one woman and one expert on child matters.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, who provides the Secretary and other staff for the secretarial support of the Child Welfare Committee?
e: The District Child Protection Unit provides a Secretary and other necessary staff for the Committee.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, what is the maximum period for which a person may be appointed as a Child Welfare Committee member?
e: No individual may be appointed as a CWC member for a period exceeding three years.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, to whom does the Child Welfare Committee submit its reports?
e: The Committee submits its reports to the District Magistrate, who conducts a quarterly review.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, how often does the District Magistrate review the Child Welfare Committee's activities?
e: The District Magistrate conducts a quarterly review of the Committee's activities.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, for at least how many days a month must the Child Welfare Committee convene?
e: The Committee must convene for at least twenty days a month.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, how many Child Welfare Committee members, at minimum, must be present at the final disposal of a case?
e: At least three members must be present at the final disposal of a case by the Committee.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, if there is no majority opinion among Child Welfare Committee members, whose opinion prevails?
e: If there is no majority among CWC members, the Chairperson's opinion shall stand.

q: Which section of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 gives the Child Welfare Committee authority to dispose of cases for care, treatment, and rehabilitation of children in need of care and protection?
e: Section 29 gives the Committee authority to dispose of such cases.

q: Which section of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 lists the functions and responsibilities of the Child Welfare Committee?
e: Section 30 deals with the functions and responsibilities of the Child Welfare Committee.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, the Child Welfare Committee must conduct at least how many inspections per month of residential facilities for children in need of care and protection?
e: The Committee must conduct at least two inspections per month of such residential facilities.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, how many committee members at minimum may decide to take suo motu cases against those who fail to produce a child before the committee?
e: A committee with at least three members may decide to take suo motu cases in such situations.

q: Which chapter of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 deals with the procedures related to children in need of care and protection?
e: Chapter VI deals with the procedure in relation to children in need of care and protection.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, within how many hours must a child in need of care and protection be produced before the Child Welfare Committee?
e: Such a child must be produced before the committee within 24 hours.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, failing to report information about a child found lost, abandoned, or orphaned within the stipulated time is considered an offense under which section?
e: Section 33 makes failure to report such information within the stipulated time an offense.

q: Under Section 34 of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, what is the penalty for failing to report information about a child within the stipulated time?
o: Imprisonment up to 3 months or a fine up to 5,000 rupees
Imprisonment up to 6 months or a fine up to 10,000 rupees
Imprisonment up to 1 year or a fine up to 50,000 rupees
A fine only, up to 1,000 rupees
e: Section 34 prescribes imprisonment up to six months or a fine up to ten thousand rupees, or both.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, if a parent or guardian is directed to surrender a child before the Committee, what period are they given to reconsider their decision?
e: The parent or guardian is given a period of two months to reconsider their decision to surrender the child.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, within how many days must the social inquiry into a child be completed, with a final order issued within how many months (Section 36)?
e: Under Section 36, the social inquiry must be completed within 15 days and the committee's final order issued within 4 months.

q: Which section of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 deals with the rehabilitation of children in need of care and protection?
e: Section 40 deals with the rehabilitation of children in need of care and protection.

q: Which section of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 deals with the registration of child care institutions?
e: Section 41 deals with the registration of child care institutions.

q: Under Section 42 of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, what is the penalty for running an unregistered institution housing children?
o: Imprisonment up to 1 year or a fine of not less than 1 lakh rupees, or both
A fine only, up to 10,000 rupees
Imprisonment up to 3 years or a fine up to 5 lakh rupees
e: The person in charge of an unregistered institution is liable to imprisonment up to one year or a fine of not less than one lakh rupees, or both.

q: Which section of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 deals with Open Shelters?
e: Section 43 deals with Open Shelters.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, what is the primary duty of an Open Shelter?
o: To protect children in difficult circumstances from abuse and save them from life on the streets
e: Open shelters are meant to protect children in difficult circumstances from abuse and save them from a life on the streets.

q: Which section of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 deals with Foster Care?
e: Section 44 deals with Foster Care.

q: Which section of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 deals with Observation Homes?
e: Section 47 deals with Observation Homes.

q: What is the purpose of an Observation Home under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015?
o: Temporary accommodation for children in conflict with law
Long-term rehabilitation of children with disabilities
e: An Observation Home is intended to temporarily accommodate children in conflict with the law.

q: Where is the main Government Observation Home in Kerala located?
e: The main Government Observation Home functioning in Kerala is located at Kollam Beach Road.

q: Which section of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 deals with Special Homes?
e: Section 48 deals with Special Homes.

q: What is the purpose of Special Homes under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015?
o: Rehabilitation of children found in conflict with law by Board order
Temporary holding of children before trial
e: Special Homes are meant for the rehabilitation of children found to be in conflict with the law by an order of the Juvenile Justice Board.

q: Where are the main Special Homes operating in Kerala located?
e: The main Special Homes in Kerala operate in Thiruvananthapuram and Kozhikode.

q: A 'Place of Safety' under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 is meant to accommodate which group?
o: Persons above 18, or children 16-18 accused of heinous crimes
e: A Place of Safety accommodates persons above 18 years of age or children between 16 and 18 accused of serious/heinous crimes.

q: Where is the Place of Safety operating in Kerala located?
e: The Place of Safety operating in Kerala is located in Thrissur.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, what are Children's Homes also known as?
e: Children's Homes under the Act are also known as Shishu Bhavan.

q: Where is the Children's Home for boys located in Kerala, as referenced in the Juvenile Justice Act notes?
e: The Children's Home for boys is located at Kollam Beach Road.

q: Where is the Children's Home for girls located in Kerala, as referenced in the Juvenile Justice Act notes?
e: The Children's Home for girls is located at Shakthikulangara.

q: Which sections of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 deal with Fit Facility and Fit Person respectively (as referenced for children's homes)?
e: Section 51 deals with Fit Facility and Section 52 deals with Fit Person.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, a children's committee must be formed in institutions to ensure participation of children above what age?
e: A children's committee must ensure participation of children above 8 years in the institution's activities.

q: Which section of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 deals with Adoption?
e: Section 56 deals with Adoption.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, which Act's adoptions are NOT affected by the provisions of this Act?
o: The Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956
e: Adoptions under the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956 are not affected by the Juvenile Justice Act.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, can a single unmarried man adopt a girl child?
o: Yes, but only with court permission
Yes, if he is above 35 years
e: A single unmarried man cannot adopt a girl child under the Act.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, in the case of a married couple wishing to adopt, whose consent is mandatory?
e: In the case of a married couple, the consent of both spouses is mandatory for adoption.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, what is the penalty if a specialized adoption agency fails to comply with prescribed adoption procedures?
o: A fine up to fifty thousand rupees
A fine up to 5 lakh rupees
e: Such an agency is liable to a fine up to fifty thousand rupees; the State Government revokes recognition on repeated default.

q: Which section of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 provides for the State Adoption Resource Agency?
e: Section 67 provides for the establishment of the State Adoption Resource Agency.

q: Which section of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 deals with the Central Adoption Resource Authority?
e: Section 68 deals with the Central Adoption Resource Authority.

q: Who is the Chairperson of the Steering Committee for the Central Adoption Resource Authority, under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015?
o: Secretary of the Central Women and Child Development Ministry
e: The Secretary of the Central Women and Child Development Ministry chairs the Steering Committee under Section 69.

q: Which section of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 deals with the powers of the Central Adoption Resource Authority?
e: Section 70 deals with the powers of the Central Adoption Resource Authority.

q: As per the Juvenile Justice (Amendment) Act, 2021, who has the power to issue adoption orders?
e: The 2021 amendment vested the power to issue adoption orders in the District Magistrate.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, what is the penalty for disclosing the identity of a child in conflict with law through media?
o: Imprisonment up to 6 months or a fine up to 2 lakh rupees, or both
A fine up to 10,000 rupees only
e: Disclosing such identity is punishable with imprisonment up to 6 months or a fine up to 2 lakh rupees, or both.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, what is the basic penalty for cruelty to a child causing unnecessary mental or physical suffering?
o: Imprisonment up to 3 years or a fine of 1 lakh rupees, or both
A fine up to 50,000 rupees only
e: The basic penalty for cruelty to a child is imprisonment up to 3 years or a fine of 1 lakh rupees, or both.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, if a child is abandoned by biological parents due to unavoidable circumstances, are the parents punished under the cruelty provision?
o: No, they are not punished under this provision
Only if the child is below 5 years
e: If biological parents abandon a child due to unavoidable circumstances beyond their control, they are not punished under this provision.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, what is the penalty for cruelty to a child if committed by a person managing or employed in an institution entrusted with the child's care?
o: Imprisonment up to 5 years and a fine up to 5 lakh rupees
Imprisonment up to 3 years and a fine of 1 lakh rupees
A fine only, up to 1 lakh rupees
e: Such a person is liable for imprisonment up to 5 years and a fine up to 5 lakh rupees.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, what is the penalty for cruelty to a child that causes permanent physical disability?
o: Rigorous imprisonment for 3 to 10 years and a fine of 5 lakh rupees
A fine only, up to 10,000 rupees
e: Cruelty causing permanent physical disability attracts rigorous imprisonment of not less than 3 years, extendable to 10 years, and a fine of 5 lakh rupees.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, what is the penalty for employing or using a child for begging?
o: Imprisonment up to 5 years and a fine of 1 lakh rupees
A fine only, up to 10,000 rupees
e: Section 76 prescribes imprisonment up to 5 years and a fine of 1 lakh rupees for using a child for begging.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, what is the penalty for mutilating or maiming a child for the purpose of begging?
o: Rigorous imprisonment for 7 to 10 years and a fine of 5 lakh rupees
Imprisonment up to 5 years and a fine of 1 lakh rupees
A fine only, up to 1 lakh rupees
e: Mutilating a child for begging attracts rigorous imprisonment of not less than 7 years, extendable to 10 years, and a fine of 5 lakh rupees.

q: Under Section 77 of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, what is the penalty for giving intoxicating liquor or narcotic drugs to a child?
o: Rigorous imprisonment up to 7 years and a fine up to 1 lakh rupees
A fine only, up to 50,000 rupees
e: Section 77 prescribes rigorous imprisonment up to 7 years and a fine up to 1 lakh rupees for this offense.

q: Under Section 78 of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, using a child for peddling or smuggling narcotic drugs is punishable with:
o: Rigorous imprisonment up to 7 years and a fine up to 1 lakh rupees
e: Section 78 prescribes rigorous imprisonment up to 7 years and a fine up to 1 lakh rupees.

q: Under Section 79 of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, keeping a child in bondage for employment and withholding their earnings is punishable with:
o: Rigorous imprisonment up to 5 years and a fine of 1 lakh rupees
A fine only, up to 25,000 rupees
e: Section 79 prescribes rigorous imprisonment up to 5 years and a fine of 1 lakh rupees for this offense.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, what is the penalty for selling or buying a child?
o: Rigorous imprisonment up to 5 years and a fine of 1 lakh rupees
A fine only, up to 50,000 rupees
e: Selling or buying a child is punishable with rigorous imprisonment up to 5 years and a fine of 1 lakh rupees.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, what is the penalty for selling/buying a child if committed by a person in actual charge of the child, such as hospital staff?
e: If committed by a person in actual charge of the child, the penalty is rigorous imprisonment of not less than 3 years, extendable to 7 years.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, what is the penalty for a first offense of corporal punishment in a child care institution?
e: The first offense of corporal punishment attracts a fine of 10,000 rupees; subsequent offenses attract imprisonment up to 3 months or a fine, or both.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, if institution management fails to cooperate with an inquiry into corporal punishment, what is the penalty for the person in charge?
o: Imprisonment not less than 3 years and a fine up to 1 lakh rupees
A fine only, up to 5,000 rupees
e: Non-cooperation with such an inquiry attracts imprisonment not less than 3 years and a fine up to 1 lakh rupees.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, what is the penalty for a militant group recruiting or using a child for any purpose?
o: Rigorous imprisonment up to 7 years and a fine of 5 lakh rupees
A fine only, up to 1 lakh rupees
e: Recruiting or using a child by a militant group is punishable with rigorous imprisonment up to 7 years and a fine of 5 lakh rupees.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, if an offense under the Act is committed against a child with a disability, what is the penalty?
o: Twice the penalty provided for that offense
The same penalty as for any other child
e: If the offense is committed against a child with a disability (certified by a medical practitioner), the offender is liable to twice the normal penalty.

q: Under Section 101 of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, within how many days must an appeal against an order of the Committee or Board be filed with the Children's Court?
e: Section 101 allows an aggrieved person to appeal within 30 days to the Children's Court.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, appeals regarding decisions on foster care, sponsorship, and aftercare made by the Committee are filed before:
e: Such appeals are made to the District Magistrate.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, within how many days should an appeal under Section 101 be disposed of?
e: Appeals under Section 101 should be disposed of within 30 days.

q: Under Section 106 of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, every State Government shall constitute which two bodies?
o: A Child Protection Society for the State and a Child Protection Unit for every District
A Juvenile Justice Board and a Children's Court for every district
A State Adoption Resource Agency and a National Commission
A Special Juvenile Police Unit and a Probation Office
e: Section 106 requires every State Government to constitute a Child Protection Society for the State and a Child Protection Unit for every District.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, the Child Welfare Police Officer designated in every police station must hold a rank not below:
e: The Child Welfare Police Officer must hold a rank not below Assistant Sub-Inspector.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, the Special Juvenile Police Unit in each district and city must be headed by a police officer not below the rank of:
e: The Special Juvenile Police Unit is headed by an officer not below the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, the Special Juvenile Police Unit must include how many social workers experienced in child welfare, with what gender requirement?
o: One social worker, must be a woman
Two social workers, at least one a woman
Two social workers, no gender requirement
e: The Special Juvenile Police Unit includes two social workers with experience in child welfare, one of whom must be a woman.

q: Under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, which additional police force is included within the Special Juvenile Police Unit dealing with children?
e: The Railway Police is also included in the Special Juvenile Police Unit dealing with children.

q: Proteins are polymers of amino acids in which each amino acid residue is joined to its neighbour by which specific bond?
e: Amino acid residues in proteins are joined by the peptide (amide) bond.

q: In the animal body, proteins are the main constituents of which tissue?
e: Proteins are the main constituents of muscle and important components of milk, blood, and skin.

q: Which element, present at approximately 16%, is considered the distinguishing element of proteins?
e: Nitrogen (~16%) is the element that distinguishes proteins from carbohydrates and fats.

q: In an amino acid, the amino group and carboxyl group are both attached to which carbon atom?
e: Both the amino group (-NH2) and carboxyl group (-COOH) are attached to the alpha carbon.

q: Which amino acid has the simplest R group, a single hydrogen atom?
e: Glycine has the simplest R group, which is just a hydrogen atom.

q: How many standard amino acids are repeatedly found in proteins?
e: There are 20 standard amino acids repeatedly found in proteins.

q: Amino acids in which the amino group is attached to a carbon other than the alpha-carbon are called beta, gamma, delta, or epsilon amino acids. Are these found in proteins?
o: No, they are not found in proteins
e: Beta, gamma, delta, or epsilon amino acids are not found in proteins.

q: Standard (proteinogenic) amino acids are incorporated into proteins via which process?
e: Standard amino acids are incorporated ribosomally into proteins, unlike non-standard amino acids.

q: Which of the following is a non-standard amino acid that occurs naturally but is NOT incorporated ribosomally into proteins?
e: Cystine is a non-standard amino acid; others like 4-hydroxyproline and desmosine also fall into this category.

q: Which group of amino acids is classified as having an aliphatic side chain?
e: Glycine, Alanine, Valine, Leucine, and Isoleucine have aliphatic side chains.

q: Which amino acids have a hydroxyl (-OH) group in their side chain, as classified by structure?
e: Serine and Threonine are classified under the hydroxyl group side chain.

q: Which of the following amino acids has an aromatic side chain?
e: Tryptophan, along with Phenylalanine and Tyrosine, has an aromatic side chain.

q: Which amino acids are classified as sulphur-containing?
e: Cysteine and Methionine are the sulphur-containing amino acids.

q: Which of the following amino acids is classified as basic, having an extra -NH2 group?
e: Lysine, along with Arginine and Histidine, is a basic amino acid.

q: Which of the following amino acids is classified as acidic, due to a -COOH group?
e: Glutamate (Glutamic acid), along with Aspartate, is classified as an acidic amino acid.

q: Which amino acids belong to the amide group classification?
e: Asparagine and Glutamine belong to the amide group classification.

q: Which amino acid is classified as an imino acid?
e: Proline is classified as an imino acid.

q: Based on polarity of the R group, which of the following is classified as a positively charged (basic) amino acid?
e: Lysine, Arginine, and Histidine are positively charged (basic) amino acids based on R-group polarity.

q: Based on nutritional requirement, which of the following groups lists all essential amino acids?
o: Valine, Isoleucine, Leucine, Lysine, Methionine, Phenylalanine, Threonine, Tryptophan
e: The 8 essential amino acids are Valine, Isoleucine, Leucine, Lysine, Methionine, Phenylalanine, Threonine, and Tryptophan, remembered by the mnemonic PVT TIM HaLL.

q: What is the mnemonic used to remember the essential amino acids?
e: PVT TIM HaLL is the mnemonic for the 8 essential amino acids.

q: Which amino acids are classified as semi-essential, becoming essential during growth, pregnancy, or recovery from trauma?
e: Arginine and Histidine are semi-essential amino acids.

q: Approximately how many non-essential amino acids can the human body synthesise?
e: The body can synthesise about 10 non-essential amino acids, including glycine, alanine, and serine.

q: Based on metabolic fate, which amino acids are described as 'purely ketogenic'?
e: Leucine and Lysine are purely ketogenic amino acids.

q: Which amino acids are classified as both glucogenic and ketogenic?
e: Isoleucine, Phenylalanine, Tryptophan, and Tyrosine are classified as both glucogenic and ketogenic.

q: Tyrosine serves as the precursor for which of the following?
o: Thyroid hormones, epinephrine, norepinephrine, and melanin
e: Tyrosine is a specialised precursor for thyroid hormones, epinephrine, norepinephrine, and melanin.

q: Which amino acid is referred to as the 21st amino acid?
e: Selenocysteine (Sec, U) is referred to as the 21st amino acid.

q: Pyrrolysine, a newly discovered amino acid, is found in which organisms?
e: Pyrrolysine (Pyl, O) is present in some bacteria and archaea.

q: For all common amino acids except one, the alpha-carbon is a chiral centre because it is bonded to four different groups. Which amino acid is the exception?
e: Glycine is the exception; its alpha-carbon is not a chiral centre because it lacks four different groups.

q: Two non-superimposable mirror-image forms of a chiral molecule are called:
e: Non-superimposable mirror-image forms are called enantiomers.

q: The DL system of classifying amino acid configuration relates the alpha-carbon configuration to which reference compound?
e: The DL system relates the configuration of the alpha-carbon to the 3-carbon aldose glyceraldehyde.

q: All amino acids ribosomally incorporated into proteins are of which configuration?
e: All amino acids incorporated ribosomally into proteins are of L-configuration.

q: D-configuration amino acids are found in which of the following?
e: D-configuration is seen in antibiotics and peptidoglycan (bacterial cell wall).

q: In the RS system of amino acid stereochemistry, which substituent has the highest priority?
e: The priority order is SH > OH > NH2 > COOH > CH2OH > CH3 > H, with SH having the highest priority.

q: In the RS system, clockwise rotation of substituent priority corresponds to which configuration?
e: Clockwise rotation corresponds to the R configuration; anticlockwise corresponds to S.

q: Which of the following amino acids is known to be tasteless?
e: Tyrosine is tasteless, while glycine and alanine are sweet.

q: Amino acids generally have melting points above what temperature?
e: Amino acids have high melting points, above 200 °C.

q: A substance that rotates plane-polarised light clockwise is called:
e: Clockwise rotation of plane-polarised light is called dextrorotatory (+/d); counter-clockwise is levorotatory (-/l).

q: Which amino acid is the only one that is NOT optically active?
e: All amino acids except glycine are optically active, due to the chiral alpha-carbon.

q: At physiological pH (7.4), an amino acid exists predominantly as a:
o: Neutral, uncharged molecule with no ions
e: At physiological pH, the amino group is protonated and the carboxyl group is deprotonated, forming a zwitterion.

q: The isoelectric point (pI) of an amino acid is defined as:
o: The pH at which it is most soluble
The pH at which the molecule exists as a zwitterion with no net charge
The pH at which it denatures
e: The isoelectric point is the pH at which the amino acid exists as a zwitterion with no net charge.

q: The isoelectric point (pI) of leucine is approximately:
e: Leucine has a pI of approximately 6.0.

q: Decarboxylation of histidine produces which amine?
e: Decarboxylation of histidine produces histamine.

q: Decarboxylation of lysine produces which compound?
e: Decarboxylation of lysine produces cadaverine, along with CO2.

q: In the ninhydrin reaction, the reaction of ammonia with ninhydrin produces a deep blue compound known as:
e: NH3 reacting with ninhydrin produces Ruhemann's purple (diketohydrin), seen as deep blue.

q: In the ninhydrin reaction, which amino acid gives a yellow colour instead of the typical blue?
e: Proline and other imino acids give a yellow colour in the ninhydrin reaction, while asparagine gives brown.

q: Transamination, the transfer of an amino group from an amino acid to a keto acid, is catalysed by which enzyme, with which coenzyme?
e: Transamination is catalysed by transaminase using pyridoxal phosphate as a coenzyme.

q: 4-Hydroxyproline and 5-hydroxylysine, derived from proline and lysine respectively, are found mainly in which protein?
e: 4-Hydroxyproline and 5-hydroxylysine are found in collagen; hydroxyproline is also found in plant cell-wall proteins.

q: 6-N-Methyllysine is a constituent of which protein?
e: 6-N-Methyllysine is a constituent of myosin.

q: Gamma-carboxyglutamate is found in which blood-clotting protein?
e: Gamma-carboxyglutamate is found in prothrombin and Ca2+-binding proteins.

q: Desmosine, a derivative of four lysine residues, is found in which protein?
e: Desmosine is found in elastin.

q: Cystine is formed by the combination of which two amino acid molecules?
o: Two cysteine molecules via a disulphide bond
e: Cystine is formed by the combination of two cysteine molecules through a disulphide bond.

q: D-serine and D-aspartate, unusual D-configuration amino acids, are found in which tissue?
e: D-serine and D-aspartate are found in brain tissue.

q: Ornithine and citrulline, though not found in proteins, are intermediates in which metabolic pathway?
e: Ornithine and citrulline are intermediates in arginine biosynthesis and the urea cycle.

q: A peptide is generally defined as a chain of how many amino acid residues?
e: Peptides consist of 2-50 amino acid residues linked by peptide bonds.

q: The formation of a peptide bond between two amino acids occurs by removal of which molecule?
e: A peptide bond forms by removal of water (dehydration/condensation) between the carboxyl and amino groups.

q: Which configuration of the peptide bond is found in proteins, due to greater stability?
e: All peptide bonds in proteins are trans, as cis is less stable due to steric clashes.

q: A chain of more than 50 amino acid residues is called a:
e: More than 50 residues constitute a polypeptide; one or more polypeptides make a protein.

q: In a polypeptide chain, which end is referred to as the N-terminal?
o: The left end, with the first amino acid
The right end, with the last amino acid
Whichever end has a free carboxyl group
e: The left end of the chain, bearing the first amino acid, is the N-terminal.

q: The primary structure of a protein refers to:
o: The sequence of amino acids held by peptide bonds
e: Primary structure is the amino acid sequence held together by peptide bonds, determined by genes.

q: Secondary structure of a protein is stabilised mainly by:
o: Hydrogen bonds between carbonyl O and amide H
e: Secondary structure is stabilised by hydrogen bonds between the carbonyl oxygen and amide hydrogen of the main chain.

q: The alpha-helix structure of proteins was proposed by:
e: The alpha-helix was proposed by Pauling and Corey.

q: All alpha-helices found in proteins are:
o: A mix of left and right-handed equally
e: All alpha-helices in proteins are right-handed.

q: Which amino acid is known as a helix breaker due to steric clash?
e: Valine, along with threonine and isoleucine, is a helix breaker due to steric clash; proline, serine, aspartate, and asparagine also break helices.

q: In the beta-pleated sheet structure, which arrangement is more stable?
o: Neither is stable without disulfide bonds
e: The antiparallel beta-sheet arrangement is more stable than the parallel arrangement.

q: A beta-turn in protein secondary structure typically involves how many amino acid residues and forms a hydrogen bond between which positions?
e: A beta-turn involves 4 amino acid residues with a hydrogen bond between positions i and i+3.

q: The tertiary structure of a protein refers to:
o: The functional 3-D shape of a single polypeptide
The arrangement of multiple polypeptide subunits
e: Tertiary structure is the functional 3-D shape of a single polypeptide chain.

q: Disulfide bridges, which help stabilise tertiary structure, are strong covalent bonds formed between which residues?
e: Disulfide bridges form between nearby cysteine residues.

q: Quaternary structure refers to the arrangement of:
o: Multiple polypeptide subunits into a larger complex
e: Quaternary structure is the arrangement of multiple polypeptide subunits into a larger complex.

q: Haemoglobin, a classic example of quaternary protein structure, is composed of which subunits?
e: Haemoglobin's quaternary structure consists of 2 alpha and 2 beta subunits.

q: Proteins are classified by solubility and composition into which three main groups?
e: Based on solubility and composition, proteins are classified as Simple, Conjugated, and Derived.

q: Simple proteins, on hydrolysis, yield only:
o: Amino acids plus a non-protein group
e: Simple proteins yield only amino acids on hydrolysis.

q: Albumins, a type of simple globular protein, are deficient in which amino acid?
e: Albumins are deficient in glycine. Examples include serum albumin and ovalbumin (egg white).

q: Globulins, a type of simple globular protein, are deficient in which amino acid?
e: Globulins are deficient in methionine. Examples include serum globulin, fibrinogen, and myosin.

q: Prolamins, such as gliadin (wheat) and zein (corn), are soluble in which solvent and deficient in which amino acid?
o: Soluble in 70-80% alcohol, deficient in lysine
Soluble in water, deficient in methionine
Soluble in dilute acid, deficient in glycine
Insoluble in all solvents, deficient in arginine
e: Prolamins are soluble in 70-80% alcohol and are deficient in lysine.

q: Glutelins, such as glutenin (wheat), are soluble in which solvent?
e: Glutelins are insoluble in water and alcohol but soluble in dilute acid or alkali.

q: Histones, a type of simple protein, are rich in which amino acid?
e: Histones are basic proteins rich in histidine, e.g., the globin of haemoglobin.

q: Protamines, the simplest simple proteins, are rich in which amino acid and lack which two amino acids?
o: Rich in arginine; lack Tyrosine and Tryptophan
Rich in lysine; lack Glycine and Alanine
Rich in histidine; lack Methionine and Cysteine
Rich in glycine; lack Lysine and Arginine
e: Protamines are rich in arginine and lack tyrosine and tryptophan; found in the sperm of certain fish.

q: Albuminoids (scleroproteins), a type of fibrous protein, are notable for their stability and are found in which structures?
e: Albuminoids show great stability and insolubility, found in hair, horn, and nails.

q: Collagen, a fibrous protein lacking which amino acid, yields gelatin on boiling with water or dilute acid?
e: Collagen lacks tryptophan and yields gelatin when boiled with water or dilute acid.

q: Elastins, fibrous proteins found in elastic tissues, are mainly located in:
e: Elastins are found in elastic tissues such as tendons and arteries.

q: Human hair keratin can contain cysteine content up to what percentage?
e: Human hair keratin can have up to 14% cysteine content.

q: Conjugated proteins consist of a simple protein combined with which additional component?
e: Conjugated (compound) proteins consist of a simple protein plus a non-protein prosthetic group.

q: Nucleoproteins, a class of conjugated protein, have which prosthetic group?
e: Nucleoproteins have nucleic acids as their prosthetic group, found in nuclei and chromatin.

q: Casein, the milk protein, is classified as which type of conjugated protein?
e: Casein is a phosphoprotein, with phosphoric acid attached to serine.

q: Haemoglobin, a conjugated protein, is classified as a:
e: Haemoglobin is a chromoprotein (with a coloured prosthetic group), along with flavoprotein and cytochrome.

q: Transferrin and Ceruloplasmin are examples of which class of conjugated protein?
e: Transferrin (binds Fe) and Ceruloplasmin (binds Cu) are metalloproteins.

q: Derived proteins are produced through which process?
o: Hydrolysis by acid, alkali, or enzyme
De novo synthesis from amino acids
e: Derived proteins result from hydrolysis of proteins by acid, alkali, or enzyme.

q: Among secondary-derived proteins, which is the correct order of progressive hydrolysis by decreasing molecular weight?
e: The correct order of progressive hydrolysis is Proteoses → Peptones → Peptides.

q: Based on function, enzymes form the largest class of proteins. Approximately how many enzymes are known?
e: Enzymes form the largest functional class of proteins, with about 2000 known.

q: Which of the following is an example of a regulatory protein (hormone)?
e: Insulin is a regulatory hormone protein; growth hormone is another example.

q: Which proteins serve a protective function by combining with antigens?
e: Immunoglobulins (antibodies) combine with antigens for defence.

q: Storage proteins, such as globulins in pulses and prolamins in cereals, primarily serve to:
o: Store amino acids for embryo growth
e: Storage proteins store amino acids for use during embryo development and growth.

q: Which proteins are responsible for transporting oxygen in blood and muscle, respectively?
e: Haemoglobin transports oxygen in blood; myoglobin transports oxygen in muscle.

q: Ricin (from castor) and snake venom are examples of which functional class of protein?
e: Ricin and snake venom belong to the toxic protein functional class.

q: Antifreeze glycoproteins, an 'exotic' functional class of protein, are found in which organism?
e: Antifreeze glycoproteins are found in Antarctic fish, helping them survive in water as cold as -1.9°C.

q: Fibroin, the protein secreted for silk and spider webs, belongs to which functional class?
e: Fibroin is classified under the secretory functional class of proteins.

q: Based on nutritional value, a 'complete' or 'first-class' protein is one that:
o: Contains all essential amino acids in required proportion and supports growth
Lacks one essential amino acid but maintains adults
e: Complete proteins contain all essential amino acids in the required proportion and support growth, e.g., casein of milk.

q: Pulses are nutritionally classified as incomplete proteins because they lack which essential amino acid?
e: Pulses lack methionine, while cereals lack lysine; combining both achieves protein complementation.

q: Zein, the protein from corn, is considered a 'poor' protein nutritionally because it lacks which two essential amino acids?
e: Zein lacks tryptophan and lysine, making it a poor-quality protein that cannot maintain body weight alone.

q: The molecular weight of proteins typically ranges from approximately:
e: Protein molecular weight typically ranges from about 5x10^3 to 1x10^6 daltons.

q: The light-scattering property of colloidal protein solutions is known as the:
e: The Tyndall effect describes light scattering caused by the colloidal nature of protein solutions.

q: Denaturation of a protein refers to disruption of which structural levels, leading to loss of biological activity?
e: Denaturation disrupts secondary and tertiary structure, leading to loss of biological activity, often followed by coagulation.

q: At the isoelectric point (pI), a protein's solubility, osmotic pressure, and viscosity are at their:
e: At pI, solubility, osmotic pressure, and viscosity are all at their minimum, and the protein precipitates readily.

q: The phenomenon where NaCl increases globulin solubility is called:
e: 'Salting-in' refers to NaCl increasing globulin solubility, in contrast to 'salting-out' with high ammonium sulfate.

q: All protein solutions exhibit which type of optical activity?
e: All protein solutions are levorotatory, rotating plane-polarised light to the left.

q: The Biuret test, which produces a violet/purple colour, detects the presence of:
e: The Biuret test gives a violet/purple colour for compounds with two or more peptide linkages (i.e., proteins, not dipeptides).

q: The Ninhydrin test for proteins produces a blue colour and detects:
e: The Ninhydrin test detects free alpha-amino acids, giving a blue colour.

q: The Xanthoproteic test, giving a yellow/orange colour, detects which group of amino acids?
e: The Xanthoproteic test detects aromatic amino acids like phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan.

q: Millon's test, producing a red colour, is specific for which amino acid?
e: Millon's test gives a red colour specific to tyrosine's phenolic group.

q: The Hopkins-Cole test, producing a violet ring, detects which amino acid's indole ring?
e: The Hopkins-Cole test detects tryptophan via its indole ring, producing a violet ring.

q: The Sakaguchi test, giving an intense red colour, detects the guanidino group present in which amino acid?
e: The Sakaguchi test detects arginine's guanidino group, producing an intense red colour.

q: The Nitroprusside test and the Sulphur (lead) test both detect which amino acid, via its sulfhydryl group?
e: Both the Nitroprusside test (red colour) and the Sulphur/lead test (black precipitate) detect cysteine's sulfhydryl group.

q: The Pauly's test, giving a red colour, detects the imidazole ring of which amino acid (or tyrosine)?
e: Pauly's test detects histidine's imidazole ring (or tyrosine), producing a red colour.

q: The Ehrlich test, giving a blue colour, is specific for which amino acid?
e: The Ehrlich test detects tryptophan, producing a blue colour.

q: What is the adult Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) for protein, per kg of body weight per day?
e: The adult RDA for protein is 0.8 g per kg body weight per day.

q: As per the protein RDA table, what is the requirement (g/kg/day) for infants aged 7-12 months?
e: Infants aged 7-12 months require 1.20 g/kg/day of protein, for both males and females.

q: As per the protein RDA table, what is the requirement (g/kg/day) for children aged 1-3 years?
e: Children aged 1-3 years require 1.05 g/kg/day of protein.

q: As per the protein RDA table, what is the requirement (g/kg/day) for children aged 4-8 years and 9-13 years?
e: Both the 4-8 year and 9-13 year age groups require 0.95 g/kg/day of protein.

q: As per the protein RDA table, what is the requirement (g/kg/day) for adolescents aged 14-18 years?
e: Adolescents aged 14-18 years require 0.85 g/kg/day of protein.

q: Approximately how much protein is contributed daily by endogenous sources such as desquamated mucosal cells?
e: Desquamated mucosal cells contribute approximately 50 g/day of endogenous protein.

q: Total endogenous protein from desquamated cells and digestive enzymes/glycoproteins is approximately how much per day, mostly re-digested and absorbed?
e: Total endogenous protein contribution is approximately 70 g/day, mostly re-digested and absorbed.

q: Among dietary (exogenous) animal protein sources, which of the following is generally excluded as it has very low protein content?
e: Butter, sour cream, and cream cheese are excluded from animal protein sources as they contain little protein.

q: Enzymes that cleave bonds via hydrolysis are classified as:
e: Hydrolases are the class of enzymes that cleave bonds through hydrolysis.

q: Insulin, a protein hormone, is structurally composed of:
o: Two chains connected by a disulfide bond
Three chains with no disulfide bonds
e: Insulin consists of two chains connected by a disulfide bond, unlike glucagon, PTH, and calcitonin, which are single-chain hormones.

q: Melatonin, a hormone, is synthesised from which amino acid?
e: Melatonin is synthesised from tryptophan, while tyrosine gives rise to catecholamines and thyroid hormones.

q: Collagen, a key structural protein, is composed of how many tropocollagen chains and is especially rich in which amino acids?
o: 2 chains, rich in lysine and arginine
3 chains, rich in glycine and proline
e: Collagen consists of 3 tropocollagen chains and is rich in glycine and proline; it also contains hydroxylysine and hydroxyproline.

q: Immunoglobulins (antibodies), which are Y-shaped proteins, are made up of how many polypeptide chains?
e: Immunoglobulins have 4 chains: 2 light chains and 2 heavy chains, made by plasma cells from B-lymphocytes.

q: How many classes of immunoglobulins (Ig) are there?
e: There are 5 classes of immunoglobulins: IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE, and IgD.

q: The Na+/K+-ATPase pump, a transport protein, moves how many sodium and potassium ions per cycle?
e: The Na+/K+-ATPase pump moves 3 Na+ ions out and 2 K+ ions in per cycle.

q: Which transport protein carries vitamin A in the blood?
e: Transthyretin, also called prealbumin, transports vitamin A in the blood.

q: As a buffer protein, normal blood pH is maintained within which range?
e: Blood pH is maintained within the range of 7.35-7.45, buffered partly by haemoglobin and plasma proteins.

q: A loss of plasma albumin reduces osmotic pressure, causing fluid to leak into the interstitium, a condition known as:
e: Reduced osmotic pressure due to low plasma albumin causes fluid leakage into tissues, resulting in oedema.

q: In the digestive system, where does appreciable protein digestion begin?
e: Protein digestion begins appreciably in the stomach; there is no significant digestion in the mouth or oesophagus.

q: Which cells in the stomach secrete hydrochloric acid for protein digestion?
e: Parietal (oxyntic) cells secrete HCl, stimulated by gastrin, GRP, acetylcholine, and histamine.

q: The approximate pH of gastric juice in the stomach is:
e: Gastric juice has a pH of approximately 1-2 due to HCl secretion.

q: HCl in the stomach activates pepsinogen, secreted by which cells, into pepsin?
e: Pepsinogen is secreted by chief cells and activated to pepsin by HCl.

q: Pepsin, an endopeptidase, preferentially attacks peptide bonds adjacent to which type of amino acids?
e: Pepsin is active at acidic pH and prefers cleaving near acidic and aromatic amino acids.

q: Rennin (chymosin), which curdles milk casein, is functionally significant in which population?
o: Infants and children; it is absent in adults
e: Rennin curdles milk in infants and children (forming calcium paracaseinate) and is absent in adults.

q: Acid chyme entering the duodenum stimulates the release of which two hormones that trigger pancreatic secretion?
e: Secretin and CCK are released in response to acid chyme, stimulating pancreatic secretion of alkaline juice and zymogens.

q: Enteropeptidase (enterokinase), from the brush border, converts which zymogen into its active form?
e: Enteropeptidase converts trypsinogen into active trypsin, which then activates other zymogens by autocatalysis.

q: Trypsin, a pancreatic endopeptidase, cleaves peptide bonds adjacent to which amino acids?
e: Trypsin cleaves peptide bonds adjacent to basic amino acids, lysine and arginine.

q: Chymotrypsin, a pancreatic endopeptidase, cleaves peptide bonds primarily adjacent to which amino acids?
e: Chymotrypsin cleaves peptide bonds adjacent to aromatic amino acids (Phe, Tyr, Trp), and also Met, Asn, His.

q: Elastase, a pancreatic endopeptidase, cleaves peptide bonds adjacent to which group of amino acids?
o: Small amino acids — alanine, glycine, serine
e: Elastase cleaves peptide bonds adjacent to small amino acids such as alanine, glycine, and serine.

q: Carboxypeptidases A and B are exopeptidases dependent on which metal ion?
e: Carboxypeptidases A and B are zinc-dependent exopeptidases that cleave from the C-terminal end.

q: Aminopeptidase, a brush-border exopeptidase, cleaves amino acids from which end of oligopeptides?
e: Aminopeptidase cleaves N-terminal amino acids of oligopeptides.

q: What are the main end products of protein digestion that are absorbed in the small intestine?
e: The main end products of digestion are free amino acids plus di- and tripeptides.

q: Free amino acids inhibiting brush-border peptidases is an example of:
e: This is called end-product inhibition, where free amino acids inhibit brush-border peptidases.

q: Amino acid absorption occurs along the whole small intestine but mostly in which part?
e: Amino acid absorption occurs mostly in the proximal (upper) part of the small intestine.

q: L-amino acids are absorbed by active transport, while D-amino acids are absorbed by:
e: L-amino acids use active transport (against the gradient); D-amino acids are absorbed by simple diffusion.

q: In Na+-dependent active amino acid absorption, the sodium ion is ultimately pumped out of the cell by which enzyme?
e: Na+ is pumped out of the cell by Na+/K+-ATPase, with energy indirectly supplied by ATP.

q: Which amino acids are absorbed fastest, due to higher affinity from greater hydrocarbon mass of their side chains?
e: Branched-chain amino acids are absorbed fastest due to their higher affinity from larger hydrocarbon side chains.

q: Which amino acids are absorbed the slowest in the small intestine?
e: The dicarboxylic (acidic) amino acids glutamate and aspartate are absorbed the slowest, despite being non-essential.

q: The gamma-glutamyl cycle (Meister cycle) uses which tripeptide to transport selected neutral amino acids across membranes?
e: The Meister cycle uses glutathione (gamma-glutamyl-cysteinyl-glycine) to transport selected neutral amino acids.

q: Glutathione, used in the gamma-glutamyl cycle, is composed of which three amino acids?
e: Glutathione is composed of glutamate, cysteine, and glycine, linked by an unusual gamma-carboxyl peptide bond between Glu and Cys.

q: The gamma-glutamyl cycle costs how many ATP molecules per amino acid transported, making it energetically expensive?
e: The gamma-glutamyl cycle costs 3 ATP per amino acid transported, making it an uncommon transport system.

q: Di- and tripeptides cross the intestinal brush border via which transporter, coupled to which ion?
e: PEPT1 transports di- and tripeptides, coupled to H+ co-transport.

q: Approximately what percentage of amino acids are absorbed as small peptides rather than free amino acids?
e: Peptide transport is faster than free-amino-acid transport, and over 60% of amino acids are absorbed as small peptides.

q: The intestine uses approximately what percentage of dietary glutamate, mostly for its own energy and synthesis needs?
e: The intestine uses up to approximately 90% of dietary glutamate, along with 30-40% of some essential amino acids.

q: In infants, intact proteins such as maternal immunoglobulins are absorbed briefly after birth through which process?
e: Intact proteins, including maternal immunoglobulins, are absorbed in infants briefly after birth via endocytosis/pinocytosis.

q: Proteins occur in cereal seeds and dry legumes, and in smaller amounts in which other foods?
e: Besides cereals and legumes, proteins occur in smaller amounts in potato, fruits, and vegetables.

q: Which elements are present in all proteins, with sulphur present in only some?
e: Proteins contain carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and nitrogen, with sulphur present in some amino acids.

q: Globular proteins (e.g., pepsin, insulin) and fibrillar proteins (e.g., fibrinogen, myosin) are classified based on which property?
e: Proteins are classified as globular (spherical) or fibrillar (thread-like) based on shape.

q: Proteins precipitated by heavy metals such as Hg, Cu, Ag, and Zn act, in that interaction, as:
e: Proteins act as anions when precipitated by heavy metals like Hg, Cu, Ag, and Zn.

The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act was last amended in:
e: JJ Act 2015, amended in 2021

India's first digital census was planned for:

e: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child was adopted by the UN General Assembly on 20 November 1989.

q: The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) was passed in:
e: MGNREGA was enacted in 2005, guaranteeing 100 days of wage employment per year to every rural household whose adult members volunteer for unskilled manual work.

q: The National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) was launched in:
e: NRHM was launched in 2005 to strengthen rural health infrastructure and provide universal access to equitable, affordable, and quality health care.

q: Mid-Day Meal Scheme was launched nationally in India in:
e: The National Programme of Nutritional Support to Primary Education (Mid-Day Meal Scheme) was launched in 1995 and universalised in phases.

q: The National Food Security Act (NFSA) was enacted in:
e: The National Food Security Act 2013 provides subsidised food grains to approximately two-thirds of India's population through the Public Distribution System.

q: The National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) was established in:
e: NABARD was established on 12 July 1982 on the recommendations of the Shivaraman Committee, as the apex development bank for agriculture and rural development.

q: The National Nutrition Policy (NNP) of India was adopted in:
e: India's National Nutrition Policy was adopted in 1993, providing a framework for addressing malnutrition through multi-sectoral strategies.

q: Community Development Programme (CDP) in India was launched in:
e: India's Community Development Programme was launched on 2 October 1952 (Gandhi Jayanti) by Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru, initially covering 55 Community Development Blocks.

q: The Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan (Drug-Free India Campaign) was initiated in:
e: The Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan was initiated in 2020 to reduce drug demand, targeting highly vulnerable districts through a localised, community-led framework.

q: The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act was enacted in:
e: The SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act was enacted in 1989. (Verified independently via web search — confirmed, not just sourced from the notes.)

q: The Protection of Civil Rights Act, which codifies the prohibition of untouchability practices, was enacted in:
e: Note: the source PDF's extracted text showed the year as '1555', which is almost certainly an OCR scanning error — 1555 predates the Indian Constitution and cannot be correct. The actual Act (originally the Untouchability Offences Act) was enacted in 1955 and renamed the Protection of Civil Rights Act via a 1976 amendment. This has been independently verified via web search.

q: In which year was the Central Social Welfare Board (CSWB) established?
e: CSWB was established in 1953 as India's premier social welfare organization.

q: The Central Social Welfare Board (CSWB) is funded by:
e: The CSWB is funded entirely by the Government of India.

q: Under which department is the budget and program costs of CSWB managed?
o: Department of Women and Child Development
e: CSWB budget and program costs are managed under the Department of Social Welfare.

q: Who is the Chairperson of the Central Social Welfare Board?
o: A retired IAS officer nominated by the PM
A prominent female social worker appointed by the government
The Union Minister of Social Welfare
The Secretary of the Planning Commission
e: The Chairperson must be a prominent female social worker appointed by the government in consultation with the Ministry of Social Welfare.

q: How many members constitute the General Body of the Central Social Welfare Board?
e: The General Body of CSWB consists of 51 members led by the Chairperson.

q: How many Members of Parliament are included in the General Body of the CSWB?
e: Three Members of Parliament are included in the General Body of the CSWB.

q: The Executive Committee of the CSWB is responsible for:
e: The Executive Committee (15 members) is responsible for managing the board's daily affairs.

q: How many members are in the Executive Committee of the CSWB?
e: The Executive Committee of CSWB consists of 15 members nominated from the General Body.

q: The Secretary of CSWB holds the rank equivalent to a:
o: Deputy Secretary or Director in Central Government
e: The Secretary holds the rank of a Deputy Secretary or Director in the Central Government.

q: How many Joint Directors are part of the administrative team of CSWB?
e: The internal administration is led by three Joint Directors.

q: Which of the following is NOT a statutory responsibility of the CSWB?
o: Conducting surveys to evaluate requirements of social welfare organizations
Providing financial assistance to hostels for working women
Granting permission to establish new political parties
e: Granting permission for political parties is not a function of CSWB. Its functions include surveys, grants, training, and coordination.

q: CSWB provides targeted subsidies to hostels serving:
o: Working women and visually impaired individuals
e: CSWB provides financial assistance to hostels serving working women and visually impaired individuals.

q: The primary mission of the CSWB is to:
o: Foster and advance social welfare initiatives across the country
Conduct parliamentary debates on social welfare
Manage the national social insurance program
e: The primary mission of CSWB is to foster and advance social welfare initiatives across the country.

q: Which body is described as India's premier organization dedicated to social welfare?
e: The Central Social Welfare Board (CSWB), established in 1953, is India's premier social welfare organization.

q: The Executive Committee of CSWB is nominated by the government from which body?
e: The Executive Committee members are nominated by the government from the General Body.

q: In the CSWB General Body, members are nominated by state and union territory governments along with:
o: Social scientists, social welfare administrators, MPs, and Planning Commission representatives
e: The General Body includes social scientists, social welfare administrators, 3 MPs, a Planning Commission representative, and ministry officials.

q: What is the role of CSWB in inter-agency coordination?
o: It directly controls all NGOs in India
It aligns welfare efforts of union and state governments and bridges gaps between departments and voluntary organizations
It funds state government social welfare departments
It appoints district level social welfare officers
e: CSWB coordinates welfare efforts of union and state governments, bridging the gap between state departments, voluntary organizations, and the central board.

q: Which ministry is the CSWB Chairperson appointed in consultation with?
o: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
e: The CSWB Chairperson is appointed by the government in consultation with the Ministry of Social Welfare.

q: Training and innovation responsibilities of CSWB include:
o: Facilitating social work training programs and launching experimental pilot projects
e: CSWB facilitates social work training programs and launches experimental pilot projects.

q: What does 'Grants-in-Aid' function of CSWB involve?
o: Providing tax exemptions to social welfare organizations
Allocating financial grants to NGOs and voluntary groups supporting vulnerable populations
Funding political campaigns for social welfare candidates
e: CSWB's Grants-in-Aid function involves allocating financial grants to NGOs and voluntary groups supporting vulnerable populations.

q: How many State Social Welfare Boards (SSWBs) are there in India?
e: A network of 33 State Social Welfare Boards operates from state capitals and union territories.

q: Where do the State Social Welfare Boards primarily operate from?
e: SSWBs operate out of state capitals and union territories.

q: The primary mission of the SSWBs is to implement welfare and development schemes for:
o: Women and children through registered voluntary organizations
e: SSWBs implement welfare and development schemes for women and children through registered voluntary organizations.

q: Board members of SSWBs are nominated jointly by:
o: Central Board and State Government on 50:50 ratio
Ministry of Social Welfare and NITI Aayog
e: Board members are nominated jointly by the Central Board and the State Government on a 50:50 ratio.

q: How often must the State Social Welfare Board hold full Board meetings?
e: A full Board meeting must be held at least once every quarter.

q: The Finance Committee of the SSWB must meet:
e: The Finance Committee must meet every two months to review and approve financial matters.

q: The Finance Committee of an SSWB must include representation from:
e: The Finance Committee must have representation from the state's Finance Department.

q: Upon appointment of a new Chairperson of an SSWB, what must happen?
o: All ongoing projects must be reviewed
The Central Board and State Government must reconstitute the Board without delay
A new Finance Committee must be formed first
e: Upon appointment of a new Chairperson, the Central Board and State Government must cooperate immediately to fully reconstitute the Board members.

q: The Chairperson of an SSWB is appointed by the State Government with approval from:
e: The Chairperson is appointed by the State Government with approval from the Central Board.

q: The annual tenure report of the SSWB Chairperson must be submitted to:
o: Ministry of Women and Child Development and NITI Aayog
High Court and State Finance Department
e: The annual tenure report must be submitted to both the Central Board and the State Government.

q: For years 1 through 4 of tenure, the annual report must be submitted within:
o: 30 days after completion of the preceding year
60 days after completion of the preceding year
90 days after completion of the preceding year
e: For years 1-4, the annual report must be submitted within 30 days after the completion of the preceding year.

q: In the 5th (final) year of tenure, the SSWB Chairperson must submit the annual report:
o: Within 30 days after the year ends
At least 30 days before her final tenure concludes
Within 60 days after the year ends
On the last day of the final year
e: In the final year, the report must be submitted at least 30 days before her final tenure concludes.

q: Program sub-committees of SSWBs must include:
o: Both Board members and field officers
e: Program sub-committees must include both Board members and field officers to incorporate qualitative, ground-level feedback.

q: If certain districts lack direct representation in an SSWB, coverage is provided by:
o: Nearby district members assigned to oversee those districts
District Magistrates acting as ex-officio members
e: If districts lack direct representation, nearby district members are assigned to oversee them to ensure complete geographic coverage.

q: Which of the following is a key duty of the SSWB Chairperson in inter-departmental linkages?
o: Directly funding all social welfare schemes
Establishing coordination with key State Government departments including Social Welfare, WCD, Rural Development, Health, and Education
Appointing all district-level social welfare officers
Preparing the annual state budget for social welfare
e: The Chairperson must establish coordination with key State Government departments including Social Welfare, WCD, Rural Development, Health, and Education.

q: When evaluating funding proposals for voluntary organizations, the SSWB Chairperson must ensure:
o: All districts are represented, with special priority to remote and vulnerable regions
Preference is given to organizations with the most beneficiaries
Funding is equally distributed across all districts
e: The Chairperson must ensure all districts are represented, with special priority to remote, uncovered, or vulnerable regions with low women and child development indicators.

q: Staff advances for SSWB employees (except standard field tour/TA advances) require ratification from:
e: Except for standard field staff tour/TA advances, all financial approvals require ratification from the Finance Committee.

q: SSWB Chairperson can sanction pay and progression cases for State Board personnel subject to prior clearance from:
e: Pay fixations, annual increments, and ACP cases require prior clearance from the Finance Committee.

q: Program Sub-Committees of SSWBs are established by the:
e: The Chairperson must establish specialized sub-committees for various programs.

q: Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyan (Drug-Free India Campaign) was initiated in which year?
e: Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyan was initiated in 2020 to lower drug demand across highly vulnerable districts.

q: How many highly vulnerable districts does the Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyan target?
e: The Abhiyan targets 272 highly vulnerable districts via a localized, community-led framework.

q: What does IRCA stand for in the context of drug rehabilitation?
e: IRCAs (Integrated Rehabilitation Centers for Addicts) provide counseling, medical detoxification, and social reintegration.

q: Rashtriya Vayoshri Yojana provides which type of assistance to senior citizens?
o: Free medical treatment in government hospitals
Physical assistive devices like walking aids, hearing tools, and spectacles
e: Rashtriya Vayoshri Yojana distributes physical assistive devices to BPL senior citizens suffering from age-induced frailties.

q: Rashtriya Vayoshri Yojana targets senior citizens belonging to:
e: The scheme distributes assistive devices to senior citizens belonging to the Below Poverty Line (BPL) demographic.

q: The Senior Citizen Welfare Fund utilizes:
o: Annual budget allocations from the Finance Ministry
Unclaimed institutional deposits across various central savings schemes
e: The Senior Citizen Welfare Fund uses unclaimed institutional deposits across various central savings schemes to finance experimental elderly welfare models.

q: What is the toll-free national helpline number for elder abuse cases known as Elder Line?
e: Elder Line 14567 is a toll-free national helpline providing legal counseling, emotional support, rescue linkages, and tracking for elder abuse cases.

q: Which act codifies the absolute prohibition of untouchability practices?
e: The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955, codifies the absolute prohibition of untouchability practices.

q: The Department of Social Justice funds the designation of Special Courts for expedited trials under:
e: The department funds Special Courts for expedited trials under the SC/ST Prevention of Atrocities Act, 1989.

q: Which portal implements single-window application flows for scholarship delivery?
e: The National Scholarship Portal implements single-window application flows and real-time beneficiary tracking.

q: What does DBT stand for in the context of social welfare delivery?
e: DBT (Direct Benefit Transfer) mandates electronic financial transfers directly to verified Aadhaar-seeded bank accounts.

q: DBT transfers are made to accounts that are:
e: DBT mandates electronic transfers directly to verified Aadhaar-seeded bank accounts, eliminating intermediate leakages.

q: Which portal is used alongside the National Scholarship Portal for service delivery by the Department of Social Justice?
e: The DISHA Portal is implemented alongside the National Scholarship Portal for single-window application flows.

q: Elder Line provides which of the following services?
o: Legal counseling, emotional support, rescue linkages, and tracking for elder abuse
e: Elder Line (14567) provides legal counseling, emotional support, rescue linkages, and tracking for elder abuse cases.

q: The 'Integrated Programme for Senior Citizens' finances operational expenditures of:
o: Pension offices and social security centers
Old-age homes, senior day-care centers, and specialized mobile medical units
e: The Integrated Programme for Senior Citizens finances operational expenditures of old-age homes, senior day-care centers, and mobile medical units.

q: Key operational bottleneck of the Department of Social Justice includes:
o: Resource constraints due to large target groups and fixed budgets
e: Key bottlenecks include resource constraints (large target groups with fixed budgets), implementation gaps, and intersectional challenges.

q: Data-driven adjustment in the Department of Social Justice shifts tracking from input metrics to:
o: Outcome audits using social audits, GIS mapping, and academic research
