e: The shift is toward explicit outcome audits using independent social audits, GIS mapping, and independent academic research reviews.

q: Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyan uses which approach to drug demand reduction?
o: Mass media, grass-roots community outreach targeting educational spaces
e: The Abhiyan uses mass media and grass-roots community outreach targeting educational spaces for demand reduction and awareness.

q: Which of the following best describes intersectional challenges faced by the Department of Social Justice?
o: Addressing individuals facing multiple simultaneous vulnerabilities like caste inequality, gender disparity, poverty, and disability
Coordinating with multiple international funding agencies
Reviewing the work of NGOs and voluntary organizations
e: Intersectional headwinds involve devising interventions for individuals facing simultaneous multi-layered vulnerabilities.

q: On which date was the Juvenile Justice Act 2015 passed by the Lok Sabha?
e: The JJA 2015 was passed by the Lok Sabha on May 7, 2015.

q: When did the Juvenile Justice Act 2015 come into effect?
e: The JJA 2015 came into effect on January 15, 2016.

q: Who introduced the Juvenile Justice Amendment 2021?
e: The JJA Amendment 2021 was introduced by Ms. Smriti Irani, Union Minister for Women and Child Development.

q: When was the Juvenile Justice Amendment 2021 signed by the President?
e: The JJA Amendment 2021 was signed by the President on August 7, 2021.

q: The Juvenile Justice Act 2015 has how many Chapters?
e: The JJA 2015 contains a total of 10 Chapters and 112 Sections.

q: The definition of 'After Care' under JJA 2015 relates to:
o: Rehabilitation after release from Special Home
Support system for children 18-21 years to achieve self-sufficiency
Medical care provided after a child's injury
e: After Care [Section 2(5)] is a system to help young people achieve self-sufficiency once they complete 18 years but have not yet turned 21.

q: Who chairs the District Child Protection Unit under Section 2(26) of JJA?
e: The District Child Protection Unit is chaired by the District Magistrate.

q: A 'Fit Facility' under JJA 2015 is defined as:
o: A hospital licensed for child care
A facility run by government or NGO prepared to temporarily take responsibility for a specific child
A special school for children in conflict with law
A legal court designated for juvenile cases
e: A Fit Facility is a facility run by government, voluntary organization, or NGO prepared to temporarily take responsibility for a specific child for a specific purpose [Section 2(27)].

q: The Special Juvenile Police Unit under JJA 2015 is defined under Section:
e: The Special Juvenile Police Unit is defined under Section 2(55) of the JJA 2015.

q: Under JJA, a social worker on the Juvenile Justice Board must have been actively involved in health, education, or welfare activities for children for at least:
e: A social worker JJB member must have at least 7 years experience or a degree in child psychology, psychiatry, sociology, or law.

q: Induction training for JJB members must be provided within how many days of appointment?
e: Induction training for all Board members, including the Principal Magistrate, must be provided within 60 days from the date of appointment.

q: A JJB member may be terminated if they fail to attend at least what fraction of sittings in a year?
e: A JJB member can be terminated if they fail to attend at least three-fourths of the sittings in a year.

q: At the time of final disposal of a case by the JJB, at minimum how many members must be present?
e: At the time of final disposal, at least two members including the Principal Magistrate must be present.

q: If there is a difference of opinion among JJB members with no majority, whose opinion prevails?
o: Secretary of District Child Protection Unit
e: If there is no majority, the opinion of the Principal Magistrate prevails.

q: Under JJA, who must submit the social investigation report within 15 days of first production before the Board?
o: Probation Officer (or in absence, Child Welfare Officer or social worker)
e: The Probation Officer (or in their absence, a Child Welfare Officer or social worker) must submit a social investigation report within 15 days.

q: Under which section of JJA 2015 is the apprehension of a child in conflict with law covered?
e: Section 10 deals with the apprehension of a person alleged to be a child in conflict with the law.

q: A child in conflict with law must be produced before the JJB within how many hours of apprehension?
e: The child must be produced before the Juvenile Justice Board within 24 hours of apprehension.

q: Under JJA 2015, preliminary assessments for heinous crimes must be completed by the Board within:
e: Preliminary assessments regarding heinous crimes must be completed by the Board within 3 months from the date the child is first produced.

q: For a child above 16 years committing a heinous crime, the JJB must assess:
o: Only the nature of the crime committed
The mental and physical capacity to commit the offense and understand its consequences
The child's family background and socio-economic status
The number of prior offenses committed by the child
e: The Board assesses the mental and physical capacity to commit such an offense, and the child's ability to understand its consequences.

q: Which section of JJA 2015 prohibits sentencing a child to death or life imprisonment?
e: Section 21 provides that no child in conflict with law shall be sentenced to death or life imprisonment.

q: The Child Welfare Committee under JJA 2015 is established under:
e: The CWC is established under Section 27 of the JJA 2015.

q: The CWC consists of a Chairperson and how many other members?
e: The CWC consists of a Chairperson and four other members, including at least one woman and one expert on children.

q: No individual shall be appointed as a CWC member for a period exceeding:
e: No individual shall be appointed as a CWC member for a period exceeding three years.

q: How often must the CWC convene sittings each month?
e: The CWC must convene for at least twenty days a month.

q: At the time of final disposal of a CWC case, at minimum how many members must be present?
e: At the time of final disposal of the case, there shall be at least three members present.

q: The CWC submits its reports to the:
e: The CWC submits its reports to the District Magistrate.

q: The penalty for failing to report information about a child within the stipulated time under JJA is:
o: Imprisonment up to 6 months or fine up to 10,000 rupees or both
Imprisonment up to 1 year or fine up to 50,000 rupees
e: Under Section 34, the penalty is imprisonment up to 6 months or a fine up to ten thousand rupees, or both.

q: The section of JJA 2015 dealing with open shelters is:
e: Section 43 deals with open shelters under the JJA 2015.

q: Under JJA, the social inquiry following production of a child in need of care must be completed within:
e: The social inquiry must be completed within 15 days of producing the child (Section 36).

q: The Observation Home under JJA 2015 is covered under Section:
e: Section 47 deals with Observation Homes, intended for temporary accommodation of children in conflict with law.

q: The main Government Observation Home functioning in Kerala is located at:
e: The main Government Observation Home in Kerala is located at Kollam Beach Road.

q: Special Homes under JJA are for the rehabilitation of:
o: Children in need of care and protection
Children found to be in conflict with law by an order of the JJB
Orphaned and abandoned children awaiting adoption
Children between 18 and 21 years in after-care programs
e: Special Homes are for the rehabilitation of children found to be in conflict with law by an order of the JJB (Section 48).

q: The Place of Safety in Kerala is located at:
e: The Place of Safety operating in Kerala is located in Thrissur.

q: A Place of Safety under JJA is intended for:
o: Infants and toddlers without parental care
Children in need of care and protection below 14 years
Persons above 18 years or children between 16-18 years accused of serious/heinous crimes
e: A Place of Safety accommodates persons above 18 years or children between 16 and 18 accused of serious/heinous crimes or legally in conflict with law.

q: Children's Home (Shishu Bhavan) for boys in Kerala is located at:
e: There is a Children's Home for boys at Kollam Beach Road.

q: Children's Home for girls in Kerala is located at:
e: There is a Children's Home for girls at Shakthikulangara.

q: Under JJA 2015, a single unmarried man cannot adopt:
e: A single unmarried man cannot adopt a girl child under the JJA 2015.

q: The penalty for violation of adoption procedures by a specialized adoption agency is:
e: The penalty is a fine up to fifty thousand rupees; if repeated, recognition is revoked.

q: Section 67 of JJA 2015 deals with:
e: Section 67 deals with the State Adoption Resource Authority.

q: The Central Adoption Resource Authority (CARA) Steering Committee is chaired by:
o: Union Minister for Women and Child Development
Secretary of the Central Women and Child Development Ministry
e: The Steering Committee Chairperson is the Secretary of the Central Women and Child Development Ministry.

q: After the JJA Amendment 2021, the power to issue adoption orders is vested in the:
e: Post the 2021 Amendment, the District Magistrate has the power to issue adoption orders.

q: Publishing or disclosing the identity of a child in conflict with law by any media is punishable with:
o: Imprisonment up to 6 months or fine up to 2 lakh rupees or both
Warning and cancellation of media license
e: Violation is punishable with imprisonment up to 6 months or a fine up to 2 lakh rupees, or both.

q: The penalty for cruelty to a child by a person managing an institution entrusted with the child's care is:
o: Imprisonment up to 3 years and fine of 1 lakh rupees
Imprisonment up to 5 years and fine of 5 lakh rupees
Rigorous imprisonment for 7-10 years and fine of 5 lakh rupees
Imprisonment up to 1 year or fine of 50,000 rupees
e: If the offense is committed by a person managing an institution, they are liable for imprisonment up to 5 years and a fine up to 5 lakh rupees.

q: Mutilating or maiming a child for the purpose of begging is punishable with:
o: Imprisonment up to 5 years and fine of 1 lakh
Rigorous imprisonment of 7-10 years and fine of 5 lakh rupees
Imprisonment up to 3 years and fine of 1 lakh rupees
e: Mutilating or maiming a child for begging attracts rigorous imprisonment for 7-10 years and a fine of 5 lakh rupees.

q: Under Section 77, giving intoxicating substances to a child (except on medical order) is punishable with:
o: Imprisonment up to 3 years and fine of 50,000 rupees
Rigorous imprisonment up to 7 years and fine up to 1 lakh rupees
Imprisonment up to 5 years and fine of 2 lakh rupees
e: Section 77 provides rigorous imprisonment up to 7 years and a fine up to 1 lakh rupees for giving intoxicants to a child.

q: If an offense under JJA is committed against a child with a disability, the offender is liable to:
o: Same penalty as for non-disabled children
Half the penalty provided for the offense
Twice the penalty provided for such offense
e: If an offense is committed against a disabled child, the offender shall be liable to twice the penalty provided for such offense.

q: Under Section 101 of JJA, appeals against orders of the Committee or Board must be preferred within:
e: Any person aggrieved by an order may, within 30 days, prefer an appeal to the Children's Court.

q: Appeals related to foster care, sponsorship, and aftercare decisions shall be preferred to the:
e: Decisions regarding foster care, sponsorship, and aftercare are appealed to the District Magistrate.

q: The Child Welfare Police Officer in every police station must be not below the rank of:
e: The CWPO must be at least an Assistant Sub-Inspector (ASI) with aptitude and appropriate training to deal with children.

q: The Special Juvenile Police Unit (SJPU) in each district is headed by an officer not below the rank of:
e: The SJPU is headed by a police officer not below the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police.

q: Railway Police is included in which body under JJA 2015?
e: The Railway Police is also included in the Special Juvenile Police Unit dealing with children.

q: Children's committees in institutions under JJA must be formed for children above:
e: A children's committee must be formed to ensure participation of children above 8 years in the institution's activities.

q: The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 has what Act Number?
e: The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 is Act No. 43 of 2005.

q: How many Chapters and Sections does the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 contain?
e: The Act has 5 Chapters and 37 Sections.

q: The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 came into force on:
e: The Act came into force on 26 October 2006.

q: The Domestic Violence Act 2005 received the President's assent on:
e: The Act received the President's assent on 13 September 2005.

q: Who introduced the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Bill in the Lok Sabha?
o: Maneka Gandhi, Minister for Women and Child Development
Renuka Chowdhury, Minister for Women and Child Development
Smt. Kanti Singh, Minister of State for Human Resource Development
Ambika Soni, Minister of Information and Broadcasting
e: The Bill was introduced by Smt. Kanti Singh, Minister of State for Human Resource Development, in the Lok Sabha on 22nd August 2005.

q: The Domestic Violence Act 2005 was passed by the Lok Sabha on:
e: The Act was passed by the Lok Sabha on 24th August 2005.

q: The Domestic Violence Act 2005 was passed by the Rajya Sabha on:
e: The Act was passed by the Rajya Sabha on 29th August 2005.

q: 'Aggrieved person' under the Domestic Violence Act 2005 means:
o: Any woman who files a police complaint
Any woman who is or has been in a domestic relationship with the respondent and alleges domestic violence
Any woman living in a joint family
Any woman who has been physically assaulted
e: Aggrieved person means any woman who is, or has been, in a domestic relationship with the respondent and alleges domestic violence.

q: 'Child' under the Domestic Violence Act 2005 means:
o: Any person below 18 years including adopted, step, or foster child
Any biological child of the aggrieved person
e: Child means any person below the age of eighteen years, including any adopted, step, or foster child.

q: 'Domestic relationship' under the DVA 2005 includes:
o: Persons who live or have lived together in a shared household related by consanguinity, marriage, relationship in nature of marriage, adoption, or as a joint family
Only persons living in the same household currently
e: Domestic relationship includes persons who live or have lived together in a shared household, related by consanguinity, marriage, relationship in nature of marriage, adoption, or joint family members.

q: What does Section 3 of the Domestic Violence Act 2005 define?
o: Rights to reside in shared household
e: Section 3 defines domestic violence, including physical abuse, sexual abuse, verbal and emotional abuse, and economic abuse.

q: Economic abuse falls under the definition of domestic violence under which section of DVA 2005?
e: Section 3 includes causing economic abuse as part of the definition of domestic violence.

q: Under Section 4 of DVA 2005, who can inform the Protection Officer about domestic violence?
o: Any person who has reason to believe that domestic violence has been or is being or is likely to be committed
Only close relatives of the aggrieved person
e: Any person who has reason to believe that an act of domestic violence has been, is being, or is likely to be committed may inform the Protection Officer.

q: Under Section 4 of DVA 2005, a person giving information in good faith about domestic violence:
o: Incurs no civil or criminal liability
Must be a witness in subsequent legal proceedings
e: No civil or criminal liability shall be incurred by any person for giving information about domestic violence in good faith.

q: Under Section 5 of DVA 2005, who is required to inform the aggrieved person of her rights?
o: Police officers, Protection Officers, service providers, and Magistrate
e: A police officer, Protection Officer, service provider, or Magistrate who receives or witnesses a domestic violence complaint must inform the aggrieved person of her rights.

q: The Protection Officers under DVA 2005 shall as far as possible be:
e: Protection Officers shall as far as possible be women and shall possess such qualifications and experience as prescribed.

q: Who appoints Protection Officers under the Domestic Violence Act 2005?
e: The State Government shall, by notification, appoint such number of Protection Officers in each district as it may consider necessary (Section 8).

q: The Protection Officer under DVA 2005 is under the control and supervision of:
e: The Protection Officer shall be under the control and supervision of the Magistrate.

q: Under Section 9, the Protection Officer must make a domestic incident report to the Magistrate and forward copies to:
o: The police station within jurisdiction and service providers in that area
The District Magistrate and High Court
e: Copies of the domestic incident report must be forwarded to the police officer in charge of the police station and to the service providers in that area.

q: Service providers under DVA 2005 may be registered under:
o: Societies Registration Act 1860 or Companies Act 1956
Only NGOs registered with Ministry of Social Welfare
e: Service providers may be registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 or the Companies Act, 1956 (Section 10).

q: Under DVA 2005, service providers are protected from legal proceedings for actions done:
o: In good faith in the exercise of powers under this Act
With written permission from the State Government
Under instructions from the Magistrate only
e: No suit, prosecution, or legal proceeding shall lie against any service provider for anything done in good faith under the Act.

q: Under Section 12 of DVA 2005, the Magistrate shall fix the first date of hearing within how many days of receiving the application?
e: The Magistrate shall fix the first date of hearing, which shall not ordinarily be beyond three days from the date of receipt of the application.

q: The Magistrate under DVA 2005 shall endeavour to dispose of every application within:
e: The Magistrate shall endeavour to dispose of every application within a period of sixty days from the date of its first hearing.

q: Under Section 13 of DVA 2005, the notice of hearing shall be served on the respondent within a maximum period of:
e: The notice shall be served within a maximum period of two days or such further reasonable time as may be allowed by the Magistrate.

q: Under Section 14 of DVA 2005, when the Magistrate directs counselling, the next hearing date must be fixed within:
e: Where the Magistrate has issued a direction for counselling, the next date of hearing must be fixed within a period not exceeding two months.

q: Section 17 of DVA 2005 guarantees every woman in a domestic relationship the right to:
o: File a criminal complaint against the respondent
Reside in the shared household regardless of any title or interest
Transfer ownership of the shared household
e: Section 17 provides that every woman in a domestic relationship shall have the right to reside in the shared household, whether or not she has any right, title, or beneficial interest.

q: Under Section 18, a protection order may prohibit the respondent from:
o: Entering the aggrieved person's workplace, communicating with her, alienating assets/bank accounts including stridhan, and committing acts of domestic violence
e: Protection orders can prohibit: committing DV, aiding/abetting DV, entering workplace/school, communication, alienating assets/stridhan, causing violence to dependants/helpers.

q: Under the DVA 2005, no residence order under clause (b) (directing respondent to remove from shared household) shall be passed against:
e: No order under clause (b) of Section 19 shall be passed against any person who is a woman.

q: Section 20 of DVA 2005 deals with:
e: Section 20 deals with monetary reliefs including loss of earnings, medical expenses, loss of property, and maintenance.

q: Monetary relief under DVA 2005 may include:
o: Loss of earnings, medical expenses, loss of property, and maintenance for aggrieved person and children
e: Section 20 monetary relief includes loss of earnings, medical expenses, loss of property, and maintenance for the aggrieved person and her children.

q: If a respondent fails to pay monetary relief under DVA 2005, the Magistrate may direct:
o: The respondent to be imprisoned immediately
The employer or debtor of the respondent to pay directly to the aggrieved person
The state government to pay from its funds
The Protection Officer to recover the amount
e: Upon failure to pay, the Magistrate may direct the employer or debtor of the respondent to directly pay or deposit with the court a portion of wages/salary due to the respondent.

q: Section 21 of DVA 2005 deals with:
e: Section 21 deals with custody orders — the Magistrate may grant temporary custody of children to the aggrieved person.

q: Compensation orders under Section 22 of DVA 2005 can be passed for:
o: Physical injuries and property damage only
Injuries including mental torture and emotional distress
e: Compensation orders (Section 22) cover injuries including mental torture and emotional distress caused by domestic violence.

q: An ex parte order under Section 23 of DVA 2005 may be granted:
o: On the basis of affidavit of the aggrieved person if the Magistrate is satisfied the respondent is committing or has committed domestic violence
e: An ex parte order may be granted on the basis of the aggrieved person's affidavit if the Magistrate is prima facie satisfied that domestic violence is being or has been committed.

q: Under Section 24 of DVA 2005, copies of orders passed by the Magistrate are given to parties:
e: The Magistrate shall order that a copy of every order under this Act shall be given free of cost to the parties.

q: Under DVA 2005, the Magistrate who is referred under the Act means:
o: Judicial Magistrate of the first class or Metropolitan Magistrate
e: Magistrate means the Judicial Magistrate of the first class, or the Metropolitan Magistrate, exercising jurisdiction under CrPC 1973.

q: Which Chapter of DVA 2005 deals with 'Procedure for Obtaining Orders of Relief'?
e: Chapter IV deals with the Procedure for Obtaining Orders of Reliefs.

q: Under Section 11 of DVA 2005, the Central and State Governments must ensure awareness through:
o: Public media including television, radio and print media at regular intervals
Mobile outreach programs in villages only
e: Section 11 requires governments to give wide publicity through public media including television, radio, and print media at regular intervals.

q: Section 15 of DVA 2005 deals with:
e: Section 15 deals with the assistance of a welfare expert (preferably a woman) to assist the Magistrate.

q: Under DVA 2005, if circumstances warrant, the Magistrate may conduct proceedings:
e: Section 16 provides that if circumstances warrant and if either party desires, the Magistrate may conduct proceedings in camera.

q: George Simmel was a sociologist of which nationality?
e: Simmel (1858-1918) was a German sociologist and philosopher.

q: Unlike Marx and Durkheim who focused on macro-sociology, Simmel focused on:
e: Simmel studied micro-level interactions - the patterns, meanings, and forms of everyday social life.

q: Simmel's work laid the foundation for which two branches of sociology?
e: His micro-level focus on interaction laid the groundwork for symbolic interactionism and urban sociology.

q: "Society exists wherever several individuals enter into interaction" is a quote by:
e: This is one of Simmel's most famous statements on society as interaction.

q: According to Simmel, society is best understood as:
o: A process of interaction between individuals
e: Simmel rejected the idea that society is a fixed thing, seeing it instead as a dynamic process of interaction.

q: Simmel distinguished between the "content" of interaction and its:
e: Simmel focused on studying 'forms' - the recurring patterns of how people interact, regardless of the topic.

q: Which social form involves mutual giving and receiving, such as buying groceries?
e: Exchange is the social form describing mutual giving and receiving.

q: "Casual interaction for enjoyment," such as friends gossiping or parties, is which Simmelian social form?
e: Sociability describes casual interaction undertaken for enjoyment.

q: In Simmel's social types, a person who is "part of the group but not fully accepted," such as a migrant worker, is called:
e: The Stranger is physically close but socially distant - part of the group but not fully accepted.

q: According to Simmel, the Stranger is characterized by being:
e: The Stranger occupies a unique position of nearness and distance at the same time.

q: Which Simmelian social type 'resolves conflict between two others,' such as a therapist or arbitrator?
e: The Mediator resolves conflict between two other parties.

q: Simmel's analysis of how group size affects interaction is known as:
e: Simmel used the idea of 'geometry' to explain how group size affects structure and interaction, e.g. dyads and triads.

q: In Simmel's theory, a Dyad refers to a group of:
e: A Dyad is a 2-person group, the most intimate and personal form of relationship.

q: According to Simmel, a Dyad is:
o: The most intimate/personal relationship, but unstable if one leaves
e: A Dyad only exists as long as both participate - it collapses if one leaves.

q: What happens when a third person enters a Dyad, forming a Triad, according to Simmel?
o: New dynamics like coalitions, mediation, and power shifts emerge
e: The entry of a third person changes everything, introducing coalitions, mediator roles, and power shifts.

q: Compared to a Dyad, a Triad is:
o: More stable because it can survive if one member exits
e: A Triad is less fragile than a Dyad because it can survive the exit of one member.

q: Simmel's major theoretical work linking economy with social relationships is titled:
o: The Division of Labour in Society
e: The Philosophy of Money is Simmel's major work on how money abstracts value and reshapes relationships.

q: According to Simmel's "Philosophy of Money," money:
o: Increases emotional and qualitative aspects of relationships
Abstracts value and leads to impersonal, rational, calculative interactions
Has no effect on social relationships
e: Money abstracts value, removing emotional/qualitative aspects and making interactions impersonal and calculative.

q: In Simmel's analysis, fashion reflects the tension between:
e: Simmel analyzed fashion as a way people navigate between belonging (conformity) and expressing identity (individuality).

q: Simmel's essay analyzing how urban life affects the individual is called:
e: In 'The Metropolis and Mental Life,' Simmel explored how city life affects individual psychology.

q: The "blasé attitude" described by Simmel refers to:
o: Excitement and curiosity in city life
Emotional dullness/indifference developed by urbanites to cope with stimulation
A form of rural social bonding
e: The blasé attitude is a mental defense mechanism urbanites develop to cope with constant city stimulation.

q: Unlike thinkers who saw conflict as purely harmful, Simmel believed conflict:
o: Has a social function and is part of integration, not its opposite
Has no effect on group unity
e: Simmel saw conflict as normal and necessary, capable of leading to reform, renewal, and stronger unity.

q: Max Weber, along with Marx and Durkheim, is considered:
e: Weber is considered one of the founding fathers of sociology along with Karl Marx and Emile Durkheim.

q: Max Weber's nationality was:
e: Max Weber (1864-1920) was a German sociologist, philosopher, economist, and political theorist.

q: According to Weber, "social action" is:
o: Action that takes into account the behavior of others and is oriented by it
e: Social action considers the behavior of others and is oriented in its course by that behavior.

q: A student studying to pass an exam is an example of which type of Weberian social action?
e: Instrumentally rational action is done with a specific goal using efficient means, like studying to pass an exam.

q: A person fasting for religious reasons, based on belief in a value rather than a practical result, illustrates:
e: Value rational action is based on belief in a value itself, not on the outcome it produces.

q: Crying at a funeral is an example of which type of social action in Weber's classification?
e: Affective action is action driven by emotions.

q: Touching elders' feet out of custom is an example of:
e: Traditional action is action based on custom or habit.

q: The German term "Verstehen," central to Weber's method, means:
e: Verstehen is the interpretive method Weber used to understand the meaning behind human actions.

q: Weber's concept of 'Ideal Types' refers to:
o: Analytical tools - pure/exaggerated models used to compare real situations
e: Ideal types are conceptual tools, not perfect realities, used to simplify and compare complex social realities.

q: Weber defined legitimate power, accepted by people as rightful, as:
e: When power is accepted as rightful by people, Weber termed it Authority or Domination.

q: Authority based on customs and long-standing practices, such as that of kings or tribal leaders, is called:
e: Traditional authority is based on customs and long-standing practices.

q: Authority based on personal charm or heroism, exemplified by leaders like Mahatma Gandhi, is:
e: Charismatic authority is based on personal charm or heroism.

q: Authority based on law and formal rules, such as that of government officials, is called:
e: Legal-rational authority is based on law and rules, exemplified by government officials and police.

q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a feature of Weber's 'ideal bureaucracy'?
e: Weber's ideal bureaucracy is defined by impersonality - decisions made without personal bias, not personal relationships.

q: In Weber's ideal bureaucracy, promotion and selection are based on:
e: Weber's ideal bureaucracy features merit-based selection and promotion by qualifications.

q: Weber's famous work exploring how religion influenced economic behavior is titled:
o: The Division of Labour in Society
The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism
The Elementary Forms of Religious Life
e: In this book, Weber explored how Protestant religious values shaped the growth of capitalism.

q: According to Weber's 'Protestant Ethic' thesis, which tradition especially encouraged hard work, discipline, and saving that matched the spirit of capitalism?
e: Weber argued Protestant values, especially Calvinism, encouraged hard work, discipline, and saving.

q: Weber's concept describing how people become trapped in systems of rules and efficiency, losing creativity and freedom, is called:
e: The Iron Cage describes efficiency without emotion and rules without meaning, trapping individuals like cogs in a machine.

q: "Rationalization," according to Weber, refers to:
o: The replacement of tradition, emotion, and values by logic, efficiency, and calculation
e: Rationalization is the process where logic and calculation replace tradition, emotion, and values in modern life.

q: Weber's theory of social stratification is based on which three dimensions?
e: Weber offered a multi-dimensional view of inequality based on Class, Status, and Party.

q: In Weber's stratification theory, "Status" refers to:
o: Market position based on income and wealth
Social prestige/honor based on lifestyle, caste, or religion
The ability to influence political decisions
e: Status is based on social honor, lifestyle, caste, or religion - a priest may have high status but low income.

q: In Weber's stratification theory, "Party" refers to:
o: The ability to influence decisions and control resources (political power)
e: Party represents political power - the ability to influence decisions, as seen in political parties and trade unions.

q: Emile Durkheim is widely regarded as:
o: The first person to establish sociology as an academic discipline in universities
e: Durkheim was the first to establish sociology as an academic discipline in universities.

q: Emile Durkheim's nationality was:
e: Durkheim (1858-1917) was a French sociologist widely regarded as a founding father of sociology.

q: Durkheim believed society should be studied:
o: Scientifically and objectively, like objects in natural science
e: Durkheim treated society as a real structure to be studied scientifically, like natural science.

q: Durkheim's approach of studying society using scientific methods similar to natural sciences is known as:
e: Durkheim's positivism emphasized objectivity, empirical observation, and causal explanation.

q: According to Durkheim, "social facts" are:
o: Personal choices unique to each individual
External, observable phenomena that exert coercive power over individuals
e: Social facts are ways of acting, thinking, and feeling, external to the individual, with coercive power over behavior.

q: Which of the following is given as an example of a 'social fact' by Durkheim?
e: Law and language are social facts - they exist outside the individual and existed before they were born.

q: Durkheim's 'The Rules of Sociological Method' and which other major work best illustrate his positivist approach?
e: Durkheim's study of Suicide is a landmark example of his positivist, data-driven approach.

q: In 'The Division of Labour in Society' (1893), Durkheim identified two types of social solidarity. What are they?
e: Durkheim identified Mechanical Solidarity (traditional societies) and Organic Solidarity (modern societies).

q: 'Mechanical Solidarity,' found in traditional/small societies with strong shared beliefs, is best exemplified by:
o: A modern city with diverse professions
A tribal village where everyone is a farmer with similar customs
e: Mechanical solidarity arises from similarity - shared work, values, and lifestyle, as in a tribal village.

q: "Organic Solidarity," found in modern industrial societies, is based on:
o: Interdependence between people with diverse roles
e: Organic solidarity arises from interdependence among people with diverse, specialized roles.

q: Durkheim's famous study 'Le Suicide' (1897) demonstrated that:
o: Suicide is purely a personal, biological act
Suicide is influenced by social conditions and forces
Suicide only occurs in religious communities
e: Durkheim showed that even a personal act like suicide is affected by social forces, not just individual psychology.

q: According to Durkheim, the type of suicide caused by weak social ties and isolation, such as an unmarried person living alone, is:
e: Egoistic suicide results from weak social ties and isolation.

q: The type of suicide caused by excessively strong social bonds, such as a soldier sacrificing his life for the nation, is called:
e: Altruistic suicide is caused by too-strong social bonds, as with a soldier's self-sacrifice.

q: Suicide resulting from a breakdown of social rules during sudden change, such as a businessman after a financial crash, is called:
e: Anomic suicide is caused by the breakdown of social rules during sudden change.

q: Suicide caused by excessive regulation and hopelessness, such as that of a prisoner or oppressed individual, is called:
e: Fatalistic suicide results from excessive regulation and lack of hope, as with a prisoner.

q: Durkheim's concept of 'Anomie' refers to:
o: A state of normlessness where old norms break down and new ones are not yet established
e: Anomie is a state of normlessness during rapid social change, when old norms break down.

q: The "Collective Conscience," according to Durkheim, is:
o: The set of shared beliefs, values, and moral attitudes that unify a society
e: Collective conscience is the common moral compass shared by society, telling people what is right and wrong.

q: In Durkheim's study of religion in 'The Elementary Forms of Religious Life,' he divided the world into two categories. What are they?
e: Durkheim argued religion separates the world into the Sacred (holy) and the Profane (ordinary).

q: According to Durkheim, which of the following would be classified as 'profane' rather than 'sacred'?
e: A notebook is an ordinary, everyday object - profane, as opposed to holy books, temples, or rituals.

q: Durkheim's controversial statement that crime "is normal and necessary for society" is based on the idea that crime:
o: Helps define moral boundaries and can promote social change and cohesion
Only occurs due to individual pathology
e: Durkheim argued crime defines moral boundaries, promotes reform, and can strengthen social cohesion.

q: What did Durkheim mean by 'collective representations'?
o: Shared symbols, ideas, and beliefs that represent collective experiences and social realities
e: Collective representations are shared symbols and ideas that shape how individuals think, feel, and behave.

q: "Sociology is the systematic study of collective representation" is a view associated with:
e: This definition of sociology reflects Durkheim's emphasis on collective representations as a core object of study.

q: Karl Marx's theories focus primarily on how ___ structures shape societies and social relationships.
e: Marx's theories focus on how economic structures shape societies, especially through class conflict.

q: Marx's approach laid the foundation for which perspective in sociology?
e: Marx's focus on class conflict laid the foundation for the conflict perspective in sociology.

q: The concept of 'dialectics' - understanding change through contradictions and their resolution - originated with which philosopher, whose method Marx adapted?
e: Dialectics originated with Hegel, who used it in idealist philosophy; Marx adapted the method with a materialist base.

q: Marx adopted Hegel's dialectical method but gave it a ___ base instead of an idealist one.
e: Marx's dialectical materialism views material (economic) conditions, not ideas, as the primary drivers of change.

q: In Marx's dialectical materialism, societal change occurs through the conflict of:
o: Thesis vs. Antithesis, leading to Synthesis
e: Society changes through the conflict of opposites (thesis vs antithesis) leading to a synthesis, e.g. Capitalism vs Proletariat leading to Socialism.

q: According to Marx's dialectical materialism, the primary drivers of societal change are:
e: Dialectical materialism views material/economic conditions, not ideas, as the primary drivers of change.

q: Historical materialism was developed by Marx as a response to which view, which claimed that ideas shape history?
e: Marx developed historical materialism as a response to historical idealism, arguing material conditions shape history instead.

q: According to Marx, "The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of:
e: This is one of Marx's most famous statements, opening the Communist Manifesto's first section.

q: According to Marx's stages of societal development, which stage comes immediately after Primitive Communism?
e: Marx's stages are: Primitive Communism, Slavery, Feudalism, Capitalism, Socialism, Communism.

q: In Marx's stages of development, which stage is characterized by lords owning land and serfs working on it?
e: Feudalism is characterized by lords owning land while serfs work on it.

q: According to Marx, the final stage of social evolution is:
e: Communism is Marx's final stage - classless, stateless, based on collective ownership.

q: Marx's 'Mode of Production' concept consists of two main elements: Forces of Production and:
e: The Mode of Production comprises Forces of Production and Relations of Production.

q: 'Forces of Production' in Marxist theory include:
o: Labour power, tools, machines, technology, and natural resources
e: Forces of production include labour power, tools, machines, technology, knowledge, and natural resources.

q: Under capitalism, the two main classes identified by Marx are the Bourgeoisie and the:
e: Marx identified the Bourgeoisie (owners of capital) and the Proletariat (workers) as the two main classes under capitalism.

q: In Marxist theory, the Bourgeoisie are:
o: Owners of capital and means of production
e: The Bourgeoisie are owners of capital and the means of production.

q: Marx's concept of 'Surplus Value' refers to:
o: The total wages paid to a worker
The value produced by workers over and above what they are paid, taken by the capitalist
e: Surplus value is the value produced by workers beyond their wages, forming the basis of capitalist exploitation.

q: According to Marx, 'Alienation' refers to:
o: The worker's satisfaction with their job
The estrangement of workers from their labour, product, fellow workers, and themselves
e: Alienation is the estrangement of workers from their labour, its product, other workers, and themselves.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of Marx's four types of alienation?
e: Marx's four types are alienation from Product, Process, Others, and Self - not 'Nature'.

q: In Marx's theory, the 'Base' of society refers to:
o: The economic foundation - means and relations of production
e: The Base is the economic foundation of society, consisting of the means and relations of production.

q: In Marx's theory, 'Superstructure' includes:
o: Law, politics, religion, education, and ideology
e: The Superstructure includes law, politics, religion, education, and ideology, determined by the economic base.

q: According to Marx, when the working class adopts beliefs that go against its own interests, preventing it from recognizing its exploitation, this is called:
e: False consciousness occurs when the working class adopts beliefs against its own interests, masking exploitation.

q: Marx's distinction between 'Class-in-itself' and 'Class-for-itself' refers to:
o: An objective economic position versus a class aware of its oppression and acting collectively
e: Class-in-itself is an objective economic position; class-for-itself is when the class becomes aware and acts collectively.

q: According to Marx, the 'Dictatorship of the Proletariat' is:
o: A temporary phase where the working class holds political power, abolishing private property and class
e: The Dictatorship of the Proletariat is a temporary transitional phase toward a classless society.

q: Marx's guiding principle for communism, "From each according to his ability, to each according to his ___," completes with:
e: Marx's principle for communism is: 'From each according to his ability, to each according to his needs.'

q: The term "Probation" is derived from the Latin word:
e: Probation comes from the Latin 'Probare', meaning 'to test' or 'to prove'.

q: The Probation of Offenders Act was enacted in which year?
e: The Probation of Offenders Act, Act No. 20 of 1958, was enacted on 16th May 1958.

q: The Probation of Offenders Act, 1958 applies to:
e: Section 1 states the Act applies to the whole of India.

q: According to Don M. Gottfriedson, probation is:
o: A procedure by which a convicted person is released without imprisonment, subject to court conditions
e: Gottfriedson defined probation as release by the court without imprisonment, subject to conditions imposed by the court.

q: Which Act first authorized courts to release young offenders on probation based on good conduct, expanding India's probation framework?
e: The Children Act, 1908 expanded the framework by authorizing courts to release young offenders on probation.

q: The Probation of Offenders Bill was officially introduced in the Lok Sabha on:
e: The Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 18 November 1957.

q: The Probation of Offenders Act, 1958 came into force on:
e: The Act came into force on 16 May 1958.

q: Under Section 3 of the Probation of Offenders Act, release is granted after:
e: Section 3 provides for release after admonition (a stern warning), for minor offences and first-time offenders.

q: Under Section 4 of the Probation of Offenders Act, an offender may be released on:
o: Probation of good conduct, with a bond up to 3 years
e: Section 4 allows release on probation of good conduct via a bond of up to 3 years, with or without sureties.

q: Under Section 5 of the Act, the court can order a released offender to:
o: Pay compensation and costs to the victim
e: Section 5 empowers the court to require released offenders to pay compensation and costs.

q: Section 6 of the Probation of Offenders Act provides special protection to offenders:
e: Section 6 gives special protection to offenders under 21 years of age.

q: Under Section 6, before imprisoning an offender under 21, the court must:
o: Record reasons and call for a report from the probation officer
Refer the case to the High Court
e: Section 6 requires the court to record reasons and call for a probation officer's report before imprisoning an under-21 offender.

q: Under Section 7 of the Act, the probation officer's report is:
o: Confidential, though the court may share its substance with the offender
e: Section 7 makes the probation officer's report confidential, though the court may share its substance with the offender.

q: Under Section 8 of the Act, the maximum extended duration of probation cannot exceed:
e: Section 8 caps the total extended probation duration at 3 years from the date of the original order.

q: Under Section 9 of the Act, the penalty for a first-time breach of bond conditions is:
e: Section 9 sets the penalty for a first breach of bond conditions at up to Rs. 50, with the bond continuing.

q: Under Section 12 of the Probation of Offenders Act, a person dealt with under Section 3 or Section 4:
o: Suffers full disqualification from government jobs
Does NOT suffer any disqualification normally attached to a criminal conviction
e: Section 12 removes any disqualification normally attached to a criminal conviction for those dealt with under S.3 or S.4.

q: Who can be appointed as a Probation Officer under Section 13 of the Act? Choose the option that is NOT listed.
o: A person appointed/recognised by the State Government
A person provided by a recognised society
In exceptional cases, any other person the court finds fit
e: Section 13 lists State Government appointees, recognised society persons, and in exceptional cases any person the court finds fit - not company directors.

q: Under Section 15 of the Act, a probation officer is deemed to be a:
o: Public servant under Section 21 of the IPC
e: Section 15 deems the probation officer a public servant under Section 21 of the IPC.

q: Section 18 of the Act states that it does NOT affect certain other laws. Which of the following is one of them?
e: Section 18 saves the Reformatory Schools Act 1897, Prevention of Corruption Act 1947, and State juvenile laws from being affected.

q: Under Section 19 of the Probation of Offenders Act, which provision of the CrPC ceases to apply in areas where the Act comes into force?
e: Section 19 states that Section 562 of the CrPC ceases to apply in areas where this Act comes into force.

q: Under Section 2 of the Act, "Code" refers to the Code of Criminal Procedure of which year?
e: Section 2(a) defines 'Code' as the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898.

q: Which offences are covered under Section 3 (Admonition) of the Probation of Offenders Act?
o: Offences under IPC sections 379, 380, 381, 404, 420 or any offence punishable up to 2 years
e: Section 3 applies to offences under IPC ss. 379, 380, 381, 404, 420, or any offence punishable up to 2 years.

q: Unlike Section 3, Section 4 (Probation of Good Conduct) applies to offenders with:
o: No specific restriction on previous conviction - it is at the court's discretion
e: Unlike Section 3 (first-time offenders only), Section 4 has no specific restriction on previous convictions.

q: Which of the following is a requirement under Section 4 that is NOT required under Section 3?
o: A bond, with or without sureties
e: Section 4 requires a bond, unlike Section 3 which involves only a warning with no bond.

q: Under Section 4(3), the minimum period of a supervision order by a probation officer is:
e: Section 4(3) sets the minimum supervision order period at 1 year.

q: Under Section 5(2) of the Act, compensation ordered by the court can be collected using the same procedure as:
o: A fine (under sections 386 and 387 of the CrPC)
e: Section 5(2) allows compensation to be collected as a fine, per sections 386 and 387 of the CrPC.

q: Under Section 6, which of the following reports must the court call for before imprisoning a person under 21?
o: A report from the probation officer covering character, physical and mental condition
A report from the victim's family only
e: Section 6 requires the court to call for a probation officer's report on the offender's character, physical, and mental condition.

q: Under Section 7, the court:
o: Must always disclose the full probation officer's report to the public
May share the substance of the confidential report with the offender
Must never disclose any part of the report
Must publish the report in the Official Gazette
e: Under Section 7, the report is confidential, but the court may share its substance with the offender.

q: Under Section 8(1), who may apply to the court for variation of probation bond conditions?
e: Section 8(1) allows the probation officer to apply for modification of bond conditions.

q: Under Section 8(2), if a surety refuses to agree to a proposed variation of the bond, the court may:
o: Immediately imprison the offender without further process
Demand the offender find a new surety and sign a fresh bond
e: Under Section 8(2), if the surety refuses, the court can require the offender to find a new surety and sign a fresh bond.

q: Under Section 8(3) of the Act, a probation officer can apply for:
o: Early discharge of the offender from probation due to good conduct
Transfer of the case to another court
e: Section 8(3) allows the probation officer to apply for early discharge of the bond due to good conduct.

q: Under Section 9, if the offender fails to observe bond conditions, the court can issue:
o: A warrant for arrest or summons to the offender and sureties
e: Section 9 allows the court to issue a warrant or summons to the offender and sureties for a bond breach.

q: Under Section 9, if the Rs. 50 fine for a first breach is not paid within the court's stipulated time, the court:
o: Sentences the offender for the original offence
Refers the matter to the High Court
e: If the Rs. 50 fine is not paid in time, the court sentences the offender for the original offence.

q: Which sections of the CrPC dealing with sureties are applied under Section 10 of the Probation of Offenders Act?
e: Section 10 applies CrPC provisions on sureties: ss. 122, 126, 126A, 406A, 514, 514A, 514B, 515.

q: The maximum bond period under Section 4 of the Probation of Offenders Act is:
e: The maximum bond period under Section 4 is 3 years from the date of the original order.

q: Under Section 4, conditions that can be imposed on a released offender may include:
o: Place of residence and abstention from intoxicants
e: Conditions under Section 4 can include place of residence, abstention from intoxicants, and other relevant conditions.

q: What must happen before any variation of bond conditions is made under Section 8?
o: No requirement - the court can act unilaterally
The offender and surety must be given a fair opportunity to be heard
Only the police must be informed
The variation must be published in a newspaper
e: Section 8 requires the offender and surety be given a fair opportunity to be heard before any variation.

q: Which of these best distinguishes Section 3 from Section 4 of the Probation of Offenders Act?
o: Section 3 involves imprisonment; Section 4 does not
Section 3 is a warning with no bond; Section 4 requires a bond with possible supervision
Section 3 applies only to women; Section 4 applies only to men
Section 3 has no age limit; Section 4 only applies to minors
e: Section 3 (Admonition) is a warning with no bond, while Section 4 requires a bond with possible supervision.

q: Section 3 of the Act is best described as a remedy for:
o: Truly minor cases involving first-time offenders
e: Section 3 is a simpler remedy meant for truly minor cases involving first-time offenders.

q: Under the Probation of Offenders Act, which section empowers the court to order compensation to be paid to the victim?
e: Section 5 empowers the court to order released offenders to pay compensation and costs to the victim.

q: Under Section 11, appeals against probation orders lie to:
o: The next higher court that ordinarily hears appeals from that court
e: Section 11 provides that appeals lie to the next higher court that ordinarily hears appeals from that court.

q: Under Section 11(4), can an Appellate or High Court impose a HARSHER punishment than what the original court could have given?
o: No - it cannot exceed what the original court could have given
e: Section 11(4) prevents the Appellate/High Court from giving more punishment than the original court could have given.

q: Under Section 12, a person dealt with under Section 3 or Section 4 does not suffer disqualification, EXCEPT when:
o: They are later sentenced for the original offence after release under Section 4
They are above 60 years of age
They belong to a certain caste
They live in a rural area
e: The Section 12 protection does not apply if the person is later sentenced for the original offence after release under S.4.

q: Who is the "Probation Officer" subject to control of, under Section 13(3)?
o: The District Magistrate of the district where the offender resides
e: Under Section 13(3), the probation officer is subject to the control of the District Magistrate of the offender's district.

q: Under Section 13, in exceptional cases, who else can be appointed as a Probation Officer besides a State Government appointee or a recognised society's person?
o: Any other person the court finds fit
e: Section 13 allows, in exceptional cases, any other person the court finds fit to be appointed as probation officer.

q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a duty of the Probation Officer under Section 14?
o: Help find suitable employment for probationers
e: Section 14 duties include inquiry, supervision, and helping find employment - not prosecuting the offender.

q: Under Section 15, a Probation Officer is deemed a public servant under which section of the IPC?
e: Section 15 deems the probation officer a public servant under Section 21 of the IPC.

q: Under Section 16, "good faith" acts of a Probation Officer are:
o: Protected - no suit lies against them
e: Section 16 protects good-faith acts of probation officers/Government from suit.

q: Under Section 17, State Government rules made under the Act require prior approval from:
e: Section 17 requires State Government rules to receive prior approval from the Central Government.

q: Under Section 17(3), before rules are finalized, they must undergo:
e: Section 17(3) requires 'previous publication' of draft rules to invite public feedback before finalization.

q: According to the memory aid in the "3 Ps of Probation," which of these is NOT one of the three Ps?
e: The 3 Ps are: Protect, Promote (rehabilitation), and Place (under supervised guidance) - not punishment.

q: What is the maximum imprisonment term for offences eligible for release under Section 3 (Admonition)?
e: Section 3 covers offences punishable up to 2 years' imprisonment.

q: A "presidency town" is treated as equivalent to a district for the purposes of Section 13, and the "Chief Presidency Magistrate" is treated as equivalent to:
e: For Section 13 purposes, a presidency town = a district, and the Chief Presidency Magistrate = the District Magistrate.

q: Under Section 18, which of these Acts is explicitly saved (i.e., NOT affected) by the Probation of Offenders Act?
e: Section 18 saves the Reformatory Schools Act 1897, Prevention of Corruption Act 1947, and State juvenile laws.

q: What does "admonition" mean under the Probation of Offenders Act?
o: A stern warning/reprimand, with no imprisonment and no bond
A formal apology letter published in the newspaper
e: Admonition is a stern warning or reprimand, involving no imprisonment and no bond.

q: According to the Act, who controls and can replace the Probation Officer at any time?
o: The Court or the District Magistrate
e: The Court or the District Magistrate can replace the probation officer at any time under Section 13(2).

q: What is the significance of Section 6 being described as a 'mandatory provision'?
o: The court has no choice but to consider probation for under-21 offenders before imprisoning them
The court must always imprison under-21 offenders
It applies only to offenders above 21
It is optional for the court to consider
e: Section 6 is mandatory - the court must consider probation for under-21 offenders before imprisoning them.

q: Under the Probation of Offenders Act, imprisonment for an under-21 offender under Section 6 is treated as:
e: Under Section 6, imprisonment is the exception, not the rule, for under-21 offenders.

q: Which section of the Probation of Offenders Act deals with 'Variation of conditions of probation'?
e: Section 8 deals with variation of conditions of probation.

q: Under Section 8(3), if the probation officer demonstrates that an offender's conduct is excellent, the court may:
o: Completely discharge the bond(s) and end probation early
Transfer the case to a different court
e: Section 8(3) allows the court to discharge the bond(s) and end probation early upon proof of excellent conduct.

q: The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act came into force in India on:
e: The Act received President's assent on 13 September 2005 but came into force on 26 October 2006.

q: The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 is:
e: The DV Act, 2005 is Act No. 43 of 2005.

q: How many Chapters does the Domestic Violence Act, 2005 contain?
e: The DV Act has 5 Chapters: Preliminary, Domestic Violence, Powers/Duties of Protection Officers, Procedure for Reliefs, and Miscellaneous.

q: How many total Sections does the Domestic Violence Act, 2005 contain?
e: The DV Act, 2005 contains 37 Sections in total.

q: Which Chapter of the Domestic Violence Act deals with "Powers and Duties of Protection Officers, Service Providers, etc."?
e: Chapter III covers the Powers and Duties of Protection Officers, Service Providers, etc.

q: The Domestic Violence Act, 2005 was introduced in the Lok Sabha by:
e: The Act was introduced by Smt. Kanti Singh, Minister of State for Human Resource Development, on 22 August 2005.

q: The Domestic Violence Act received the President's assent on:
e: The Act received the President's assent on 13 September 2005.

q: Under Section 2 of the Act, an "aggrieved person" is defined as:
o: Any woman in a domestic relationship with the respondent who alleges domestic violence
e: An aggrieved person is any woman who is or has been in a domestic relationship with the respondent and alleges domestic violence.

q: Under Section 2, a "child" is defined as any person below the age of:
e: Section 2 defines a child as any person below 18 years, including adopted, step, or foster children.

q: Under Section 2, "domestic relationship" includes persons related by:
o: Consanguinity, marriage, or a relationship in the nature of marriage, adoption, or joint family living
e: Domestic relationship covers consanguinity, marriage, relationships in the nature of marriage, adoption, or joint family living together.

q: Under Section 2, who qualifies as "Magistrate" for the purposes of this Act?
o: A Judicial Magistrate of the first class or Metropolitan Magistrate
e: The Magistrate under this Act is the Judicial Magistrate of the first class or Metropolitan Magistrate.

q: Under Section 3, domestic violence includes which forms of abuse?
o: Physical, sexual, verbal, emotional, and economic abuse
e: Section 3 defines domestic violence broadly to include physical, sexual, verbal, emotional, and economic abuse.

q: Under Section 3(b), domestic violence also includes harassment aimed at coercing a woman to meet unlawful demands for:
e: Section 3(b) covers harassment to coerce a woman to meet unlawful demands for dowry or other property/valuable security.

q: Under Section 4, who may give information to the Protection Officer about an act of domestic violence?
o: Any person who has reason to believe such an act has been, is being, or is likely to be committed
e: Section 4 allows any person with reason to believe domestic violence has occurred to inform the Protection Officer.

q: Under Section 4(2), a person giving information about domestic violence in good faith:
o: Incurs no civil or criminal liability
e: Section 4(2) protects good-faith informants from civil or criminal liability.

q: Under Section 5, the police officer, Protection Officer, service provider, or Magistrate must inform the aggrieved person of her right to file a complaint under which section of the IPC?
e: Section 5(e) requires informing the aggrieved person of her right to file a complaint under Section 498A of the IPC.

q: Under Section 8, Protection Officers are appointed by:
e: Section 8 empowers the State Government to appoint Protection Officers by notification.

q: Under Section 8(2), Protection Officers shall, as far as possible, be:
e: Section 8(2) states Protection Officers shall, as far as possible, be women.

q: Under Section 9, one of the duties of the Protection Officer is to make a ___ to the Magistrate upon receipt of a complaint.
e: Section 9(1)(b) requires the Protection Officer to make a domestic incident report to the Magistrate.

q: Under Section 12, when should the Magistrate ordinarily fix the first date of hearing after receiving an application?
o: Not ordinarily beyond three days from receipt of the application
e: Section 12(4) requires the Magistrate to fix the first hearing not ordinarily beyond three days from receipt of the application.

q: Under Section 13, notice of the date of hearing must be served on the respondent within a maximum period of:
e: Section 13(1) requires notice to be served within a maximum of two days from receipt, or such further time as allowed.

q: Under Section 14, if the Magistrate directs counselling, the next hearing date must be fixed within:
e: Section 14(2) requires the next hearing to be fixed within a period not exceeding two months.

q: Under Section 15, the Magistrate may secure the assistance of a welfare expert, preferably:
e: Section 15 allows the Magistrate to secure a welfare expert, preferably a woman, to assist in the proceedings.

q: Under Section 16, proceedings under the Act may be conducted "in camera" (privately) if:
o: The circumstances warrant it and either party desires
Never - proceedings must always be public
e: Section 16 allows in camera proceedings if the circumstances warrant it and either party desires.

q: Under Section 17, every woman in a domestic relationship has the right to:
o: Reside in the shared household, regardless of ownership title
Evict the respondent immediately without court order
e: Section 17 grants every woman in a domestic relationship the right to reside in the shared household, regardless of title.

q: Under Section 18, a "Protection Order" may prohibit the respondent from:
o: Committing or aiding acts of domestic violence, entering the aggrieved person's workplace, or communicating with her
e: Section 18 lists prohibitions including committing/aiding domestic violence, entering the workplace, and communicating with the aggrieved person.

q: Under Section 19, a "Residence Order" can restrain the respondent from dispossessing the aggrieved person, but the proviso states that no order directing removal from the household (clause b) can be passed against:
e: The proviso to Section 19(1)(b) states no order for removal from the household can be passed against a woman.

q: Under Section 19(3), the Magistrate may require the respondent to execute a bond for:
o: Preventing the commission of domestic violence
e: Section 19(3) allows the Magistrate to require a bond, with or without sureties, to prevent domestic violence.

q: Under Section 20, "Monetary Relief" may include compensation for:
o: Loss of earnings, medical expenses, property damage, and maintenance
e: Section 20(1) lists loss of earnings, medical expenses, property loss/damage, and maintenance as forms of monetary relief.

q: Under Section 20(2), monetary relief granted must be:
o: Adequate, fair, reasonable, and consistent with the aggrieved person's standard of living
Fixed by law at a flat rate
e: Section 20(2) requires monetary relief to be adequate, fair, reasonable, and consistent with the aggrieved person's standard of living.

q: Under Section 21, the Magistrate may grant temporary custody of a child to:
o: The aggrieved person or person applying on her behalf
e: Section 21 allows the Magistrate to grant temporary custody to the aggrieved person or a person applying on her behalf.

q: Under Section 21, if a respondent's visit to the child may be harmful, the Magistrate:
o: Shall refuse to allow such visit
e: The proviso to Section 21 requires the Magistrate to refuse a visit likely to be harmful to the child.

q: Under Section 22, "Compensation Orders" may be granted for injuries including:
e: Section 22 allows compensation for injuries including mental torture and emotional distress caused by domestic violence.

q: Under Section 23, the Magistrate may grant an ex parte order based on:
o: An affidavit of the aggrieved person, if the application prima facie discloses domestic violence
e: Section 23(2) allows an ex parte order based on the affidavit of the aggrieved person if domestic violence is prima facie disclosed.

q: Under Section 24, copies of any order passed under the Act must be given to the parties:
o: At a cost determined by the court
e: Section 24 requires the Magistrate to give copies of orders to parties free of cost.

q: Which section of the DV Act deals with 'Right to reside in a shared household'?
e: Section 17 covers the right to reside in a shared household.

q: Which section deals with 'Custody orders'?
e: Section 21 covers custody orders.

q: Which section covers 'Power to grant interim and ex parte orders'?
e: Section 23 covers the power to grant interim and ex parte orders.

q: Under Section 19(6), while making a residence order, the Magistrate may impose obligations relating to:
o: Discharge of rent and other payments
e: Section 19(6) allows the Magistrate to impose obligations on rent and other payments, considering the parties' financial needs.

q: Under Section 19(4), an order under Section 19(3) (execution of a bond) is deemed to be an order under which Chapter of the CrPC, 1973?
e: Section 19(4) deems such a bond order to be an order under Chapter VIII of the CrPC, 1973.

q: Under Section 25, a protection order made under Section 18 remains in force until:
o: The aggrieved person applies for discharge
e: Section 25(1) states a protection order remains in force until the aggrieved person applies for its discharge.

q: Under Section 26, reliefs under Sections 18-22 may also be sought in:
o: Any legal proceeding before a civil court, family court, or criminal court
Only proceedings initiated after the Act's commencement
e: Section 26 allows reliefs to be sought in any legal proceeding before a civil, family, or criminal court.

q: Under Section 27, which court has jurisdiction to grant protection orders under the DV Act?
o: The Judicial Magistrate of the first class or Metropolitan Magistrate within whose limits the aggrieved person resides, respondent resides, or cause of action arose
e: Section 27 gives jurisdiction to the JM first class/Metropolitan Magistrate where the aggrieved person or respondent resides, or where the cause of action arose.

q: Under Section 27(2), an order made under the DV Act is enforceable:
o: Only within the state where it was passed
Only in the district of the aggrieved person's residence
e: Section 27(2) makes any order under the Act enforceable throughout India.

q: Under Section 29, an appeal against a Magistrate's order under the DV Act lies to the Court of Session within:
e: Section 29 provides for an appeal to the Court of Session within thirty days of the order being served.

q: Under Section 30, Protection Officers and members of service providers acting under the Act are deemed to be:
e: Section 30 deems Protection Officers and service provider members to be public servants.

q: Under Section 31, a breach of a protection order by the respondent is punishable with imprisonment up to:
o: 1 year, or fine up to Rs. 20,000, or both
e: Section 31(1) punishes breach of a protection order with imprisonment up to 1 year, or fine up to Rs. 20,000, or both.

q: Under Section 32, an offence under Section 31(1) (breach of protection order) is:
e: Section 32(1) makes the offence of breaching a protection order cognizable and non-bailable.

q: Under Section 33, a Protection Officer who fails to discharge duties as directed by the Magistrate without sufficient cause may be punished with imprisonment up to:
o: 1 year, or fine up to Rs. 20,000, or both
e: Section 33 punishes a defaulting Protection Officer with imprisonment up to 1 year, or fine up to Rs. 20,000, or both.

q: Under Section 34, prosecution against a Protection Officer requires:
o: Previous sanction of the State Government or an authorised officer
e: Section 34 requires previous sanction of the State Government or an authorised officer before prosecuting a Protection Officer.

q: Under Section 36, the provisions of the DV Act are:
o: In derogation of all other laws
In addition to, and not in derogation of, other laws
Applicable only if no other law exists
e: Section 36 states the Act's provisions are in addition to, not in derogation of, other laws.

q: Under Section 37, who has the power to make rules for carrying out the provisions of the Act?
e: Section 37 empowers the Central Government to make rules for carrying out the Act's provisions.

q: In V.D. Bhanot vs. Savita Bhanot (2010), the Supreme Court held that:
o: The DV Act cannot apply to acts that occurred before the Act came into existence
A wife who shared a household before the Act came into existence would still be entitled to the Act's protection
Only unmarried women can seek relief
The Act applies only to Hindu women
e: The Supreme Court held that a wife who shared a household even before the DV Act came into existence is entitled to its protection.

q: In Indira Sarma vs. V.K.V. Sarma (2013), the Supreme Court ruled that:
o: All live-in relationships are automatically marriage-like
Not all live-in relationships are marriage-like, and laid down guidelines to test this
Live-in relationships have no legal recognition
Only registered marriages qualify for protection
e: The Court ruled that not all live-in relationships are marriage-like and laid down guidelines (duration, shared household, pooling of resources, etc.) to test this.

q: In Meenavati vs. Senthamarai Selvi (2008), it was held that under the proviso to Section 19, no order can be passed to remove which person from the shared household?
e: It was held that women family members cannot be ordered removed from the shared household under Section 19(1)(b).

q: In Kuldeep Singh vs. Rekha (2019), it was held that a case against parents-in-law cannot be filed if:
o: The wife is living with them
e: It was held that a case against parents-in-law cannot be filed if the wife is living separately from them.

q: Which Chapter of the DV Act is titled "Miscellaneous," covering Sections 30 to 37?
e: Chapter V, titled Miscellaneous, covers Sections 30 to 37.

q: Under Section 28, proceedings under Sections 12, 18-23 and offences under Section 31 are governed by:
e: Section 28(1) states such proceedings are governed by the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.

q: In Arvind Singh v. State of Bihar (2001), the court noted that which IPC section does not specifically address diverse forms of violence like sexual, verbal, or psychological abuse?
e: The court noted Section 498A IPC does not specifically address diverse forms of violence, giving courts wide discretion in interpreting 'cruelty'.

q: The Delhi High Court has emphasized that the Domestic Violence Act, 2005 applies to:
o: All women, regardless of religious or social background
e: The Delhi High Court emphasised the universality of the DV Act, applying to all women regardless of religious or social background.

q: The Dowry Prohibition Act was enacted in India on:
e: The Dowry Prohibition Act was enacted on 1st July 1961.

q: The Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 applies to:
o: All persons in India, irrespective of caste or religion
e: The Act is applicable to all persons irrespective of caste or religion in India.

q: Which early enactment, passed before independence by the provincial Government of Sind, attempted to deal with the evils of the dowry system but had little impact?
o: The Andhra Pradesh Dowry Prohibition Act, 1958
e: The Sind Deti Leti Act, 1939 was an early attempt to deal with dowry evils but had neither impact nor the desired effect.

q: Which two State enactments preceded the central Dowry Prohibition Act but "failed miserably"?
o: The Bihar Dowry Restraint Act, 1950 and The Andhra Pradesh Dowry Prohibition Act, 1958
The Sind Deti Leti Act and Hindu Succession Act
The Kerala Dowry Act and Tamil Nadu Dowry Act
The Punjab and Haryana Dowry Acts
e: The Bihar Dowry Restraint Act, 1950 and the Andhra Pradesh Dowry Prohibition Act, 1958 both failed miserably.

q: The Dowry Prohibition Bill was passed in:
o: A Joint Sitting of both Houses of Parliament
e: The Dowry Prohibition Bill was legally passed in the Joint Sittings of both Houses of Parliament.

q: Which of the following are amending Acts to the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961?
o: The Dowry Prohibition (Amendment) Acts of 1984 and 1986
The Dowry Prohibition (Amendment) Acts of 1970 and 1975
e: The Dowry Prohibition (Amendment) Acts of 1984 and 1986 complemented the original 1961 Act.

q: According to Section 2 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, "dowry" means:
o: Any property or valuable security given or agreed to be given in connection with a marriage
Only gifts from the bride's family
e: Section 2 defines dowry as any property or valuable security given or agreed to be given in connection with a marriage.

q: Under the Dowry Prohibition Act, "dowry" excludes mahr or dower in the case of persons governed by:
e: The definition of dowry excludes dower or mahr for persons governed by Muslim Personal Law (Shariat).

q: According to Section 3 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, who is liable for the offence of dowry?
o: Only the family of the bridegroom (for taking dowry)
Both the family that takes dowry and the family that gives/consents to give dowry
e: Section 3 makes both giving and taking dowry an offence - both families are liable.

q: Under Section 3, the penalty for giving or taking dowry is imprisonment for a term not less than:
e: Section 3 sets the minimum imprisonment for giving/taking dowry at 5 years.

q: Under Section 3, the minimum fine for giving or taking dowry is:
o: Rs. 15,000 or the value of the dowry, whichever is more
e: Section 3 sets a minimum fine of Rs. 15,000 or the value of the dowry, whichever is more.

q: Under Section 4 of the Act, the penalty for demanding dowry is imprisonment of not less than:
e: Section 4 sets the penalty for demanding dowry at not less than 6 months, extendable to 2 years.

q: Under Section 4, the maximum fine for demanding dowry is:
e: Section 4 sets the maximum fine for demanding dowry at Rs. 10,000.

q: Under Section 4-A ("Ban on advertisement"), advertising for a share in property or business in consideration for marriage is punishable with imprisonment of not less than:
e: Section 4-A punishes such advertisements with imprisonment not less than 6 months, extendable to 5 years.

q: Under Section 7 of the Act, who is competent to try an offence under the Dowry Prohibition Act?
o: A judge not below the rank of a Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of First Class
e: Section 7 requires a judge not below the rank of a Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of First Class to try such offences.

q: Under Section 7, the court can take cognizance of an offence based on:
o: Report by the victim, parents/relatives, police report, or its own knowledge
e: Section 7 allows cognizance based on a report by the victim, parents/relatives, police report, or the court's own knowledge.

q: Under Section 8, offences under the Dowry Prohibition Act are:
e: Section 8 makes certain offences under the Act cognizable, non-bailable, and non-compoundable.

q: How many total sections does the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 contain?
e: The Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 contains a total of 10 Sections.

q: Section 8B of the Dowry Prohibition Act provides for the appointment of:
e: Section 8B provides for the appointment of Dowry Prohibition Officers.

q: Under Section 5 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, any agreement for giving or taking dowry is:
e: Section 5 declares any agreement for giving or taking dowry to be void.

q: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) update India's dowry laws by replacing which older provisions?
o: IPC Section 304B and Indian Evidence Act Section 113B
IPC Section 302 and Evidence Act Section 27
IPC Section 375 and Evidence Act Section 45
e: The BNS and BSA replace older IPC Section 304B (dowry death) and Indian Evidence Act Section 113B.

q: Under Section 80 of the BNS, "dowry death" is punishable with imprisonment of:
o: Not less than 7 years, extendable to life imprisonment
e: BNS Section 80 punishes dowry death with imprisonment of not less than 7 years, extendable to life imprisonment.

q: Under Section 80 of the BNS, for a death to be classified as a "dowry death," it must occur within how many years of marriage?
e: BNS Section 80 requires the death to occur within seven years of marriage.

q: Under the BNS provisions on dowry death, the death must be shown to have occurred:
o: Naturally, with no connection to cruelty
Otherwise than under normal circumstances, preceded by cruelty/harassment for dowry
e: The death must occur other than under normal circumstances, preceded by cruelty or harassment for dowry, soon before death.

q: Which section of the BNS covers "marital cruelty/harassment" for dowry?
e: BNS Section 86 covers marital cruelty/harassment relating to dowry.

q: Under Section 86 of the BNS, "cruelty" is defined to include willful conduct likely to drive a woman to:
o: Commit suicide or cause grave injury/danger to life, limb, or health
e: Section 86 defines cruelty as willful conduct likely to drive a woman to suicide or cause grave injury/danger to her life, limb, or health.

q: Which section of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) introduces a legal presumption against the husband/relatives in dowry death cases?
e: BSA Section 118 introduces a presumption as to dowry death, shifting the burden of proof to the accused.
